## Annual Visitation Statistics Release

Annual visitor use statistics are released during the first quarter of the following calendar year. On this page you will find

*   A quick highlight of the most recent published data
*   An overview of the three main options for accessing visitor use data 
    *   **Dashboard**(quick visuals to see trends at national or park levels)
    *   **Data Portal**(also known as IRMA, comprehensive tables and reports - this is the best option for exporting data)
    *   **Abstract**(PDF document available for each calendar year of reporting - useful for references and citations)

*   An overview of data limiations and considerations

For questions or assistance, please reach out the [Visitor Use Statistics Staff](https://www.nps.gov/common/utilities/sendmail/sendemail.cfm?o=6A96D095ADE08FB284A85DA8F601&r=/subjects/socialscience/visitor-use-statistics-dashboard.htm).

## 2025 Visitation At-A-Glance

*   The National Park Service reported 323 million recreation visits in calendar year 2025. 
    *   This is a decrease of 8.85 million recreation visits, or 2.7%, from the record year in 2024. 

*   406 of the 433 National Park System units report visitor use. 
*   Two new parks began reporting in 2024. 
*   Recreation visitor hours were 1.39 billion; a decrease of 0.7% from 2024. 
*   There was a 2.4% decrease from 2024 for overnight stays. 26 parks, 6% of reporting parks, set a record for annual recreation visits.

## Visitor Use Statistics Dashboard

This dashboard includes simple line chart visualizations for the 11 official visitor use statistics. Visuals can be viewed at the monthly or annual level, and filters can be applied to see data for a specific park or designation. The data span from the most recently reported year back to 1979, the year in which every park unit began reporting monthly data for all 11 statistics. Prior to that time, only annual recreation visits are consistently available.

## Visitor Use Statistics Data Portal 

The NPS Visitor Use Statistics Program maintains a large data set with annual recreation visit estimates from 1904-1978 and monthly visitation estimates from 1979 to present. Electronic database records for all inputs and outputs have been kept since the early 1990s.

All Visitor Use Statistics data are housed within the [Integrated Resource Management Applications (IRMA) Portal](https://irma.nps.gov/Stats/). Users can chose from a set of standard reports to view aggregated [national level data](https://irma.nps.gov/Stats/Reports/National), or [park specific data](https://irma.nps.gov/Stats/Reports/Park).

#### Custom Query Builders

For a quicker more custom approach, try the Query Builder Tool, which is also available on the[National Reports](https://irma.nps.gov/Stats/Reports/National "https://irma.nps.gov/Stats/Reports/National")page in IRMA. This tool will allow users to select the years, statistics, and parks of interest, and offers the option to include some additional fields such as legacy region and unit designation.

_As noted in the data limitations there was a shift in what data were collected in 1979 so there are separate query builders based on that delineation point._  
  
[**Query Builder for Historic Annual Recreation Visits (1904 - 1979)**](https://irma.nps.gov/Stats/SSRSReports/National%20Reports/Query%20Builder%20for%20Historic%20Annual%20Recreation%20Visits%20(1904%20-%201979))  
[**Query Builder for Visitor Use Statistics (1979 - Last Calendar Year)**](https://irma.nps.gov/Stats/SSRSReports/National%20Reports/Query%20Builder%20for%20Public%20Use%20Statistics%20(1979%20-%20Last%20Calendar%20Year))

## Statistical Abstract

 The Statistics Abstract is a PDF document containing a series of tables and figures that display visitor use data for the most recently reported year. By documenting these visits across the National Park System, the National Park Service (NPS) Statistical Abstract offers a historical record of visitor use in parks and provides NPS staff and partners with a useful tool for effective management and planning. This is also a useful tool for academics and researchers in need of references and citations for publications.  
  
 The abstract is typically published mid calendar year, so there is a delay of several months between the publishing of a year's numbers and the release of the respective year's Statistical Abstract.  
  
 Download the [2024 Statistical Abstract](https://irma.nps.gov/DataStore/DownloadFile/722329).  
  

## Data Limitations and Considerations

There are several ways to access Visitor Use Statistics data. Regardless of how you choose to access the data, it does have its limitations. Please read through the following list prior to using data ensure appropriate usage and interpretation.

#### Current Year Data Warning!

Current year data are preliminary and must be thoroughly reviewed by the Social Science Program prior to being considered final. For that reason, most data are available only through last calendar year.**If electing to use current year data, please use caution as it may not be complete or controlled for quality.**

#### Reporting Changes

The way visitor use statistics have been tracked and reported has changed over time. More information related to these shifts is available on the[History and Policy](https://www.nps.gov/subjects/socialscience/statistics-history.htm)page, but here is a quick guide to what data is available for different time periods:

*   **1904-1979**| Annual recreation visits
*   **1979-1992**| Annual and monthly values for the 11 official statistics
*   **1992-Present**| Same as previous with addition of park level data inputs used to calculate official statistics.

#### Count Procedure Changes

Parks change their methods for tracking and calculating visitor use stats from time to time. This can result in trend shift in the years following a change.

#### Varying degrees of data quality

Park operations and usage by visitors changes over time for most parks.**Updating counting methods can take a great deal of time and financial resources**for the park, making it challenging to keep measurement systems completely current and accurate.

**Parks also must sometimes rely on estimated data**due to equipment failures, staffing limitations, and unforeseeable circumstances such as the COVID-19 pandemic and natural disasters.

#### Rounding Difference

Depending on the data source, data users may notice slight rounding discrepancies across different reports.

#### Potential Errors

Once the calendar year is over and data for a given year is finalized, no changes to the underlying values can be made. Some parks' data may contain permanent errors.Errors are noted in the Endnotes of the[Annual Statistical Abstracts](https://irma.nps.gov/Stats/Reports/AbstractsAndForecasts).

## Annual Visitation Statistics Release

Annual visitor use statistics are released during the first quarter of the following calendar year. On this page you will find

*   A quick highlight of the most recent published data
*   An overview of the three main options for accessing visitor use data 
    *   **Dashboard**(quick visuals to see trends at national or park levels)
    *   **Data Portal**(also known as IRMA, comprehensive tables and reports - this is the best option for exporting data)
    *   **Abstract**(PDF document available for each calendar year of reporting - useful for references and citations)

*   An overview of data limiations and considerations

For questions or assistance, please reach out the [Visitor Use Statistics Staff](https://www.nps.gov/common/utilities/sendmail/sendemail.cfm?o=6A96D095ADE08FB284A85DA8F601&r=/subjects/socialscience/visitor-use-statistics-dashboard.htm).

## 2025 Visitation At-A-Glance

*   The National Park Service reported 323 million recreation visits in calendar year 2025. 
    *   This is a decrease of 8.85 million recreation visits, or 2.7%, from the record year in 2024. 

*   406 of the 433 National Park System units report visitor use. 
*   Two new parks began reporting in 2024. 
*   Recreation visitor hours were 1.39 billion; a decrease of 0.7% from 2024. 
*   There was a 2.4% decrease from 2024 for overnight stays. 26 parks, 6% of reporting parks, set a record for annual recreation visits.

## Visitor Use Statistics Dashboard

This dashboard includes simple line chart visualizations for the 11 official visitor use statistics. Visuals can be viewed at the monthly or annual level, and filters can be applied to see data for a specific park or designation. The data span from the most recently reported year back to 1979, the year in which every park unit began reporting monthly data for all 11 statistics. Prior to that time, only annual recreation visits are consistently available.

## Visitor Use Statistics Data Portal 

The NPS Visitor Use Statistics Program maintains a large data set with annual recreation visit estimates from 1904-1978 and monthly visitation estimates from 1979 to present. Electronic database records for all inputs and outputs have been kept since the early 1990s.

All Visitor Use Statistics data are housed within the [Integrated Resource Management Applications (IRMA) Portal](https://irma.nps.gov/Stats/). Users can chose from a set of standard reports to view aggregated [national level data](https://irma.nps.gov/Stats/Reports/National), or [park specific data](https://irma.nps.gov/Stats/Reports/Park).

#### Custom Query Builders

For a quicker more custom approach, try the Query Builder Tool, which is also available on the[National Reports](https://irma.nps.gov/Stats/Reports/National "https://irma.nps.gov/Stats/Reports/National")page in IRMA. This tool will allow users to select the years, statistics, and parks of interest, and offers the option to include some additional fields such as legacy region and unit designation.

_As noted in the data limitations there was a shift in what data were collected in 1979 so there are separate query builders based on that delineation point._  
  
[**Query Builder for Historic Annual Recreation Visits (1904 - 1979)**](https://irma.nps.gov/Stats/SSRSReports/National%20Reports/Query%20Builder%20for%20Historic%20Annual%20Recreation%20Visits%20(1904%20-%201979))  
[**Query Builder for Visitor Use Statistics (1979 - Last Calendar Year)**](https://irma.nps.gov/Stats/SSRSReports/National%20Reports/Query%20Builder%20for%20Public%20Use%20Statistics%20(1979%20-%20Last%20Calendar%20Year))

## Statistical Abstract

 The Statistics Abstract is a PDF document containing a series of tables and figures that display visitor use data for the most recently reported year. By documenting these visits across the National Park System, the National Park Service (NPS) Statistical Abstract offers a historical record of visitor use in parks and provides NPS staff and partners with a useful tool for effective management and planning. This is also a useful tool for academics and researchers in need of references and citations for publications.  
  
 The abstract is typically published mid calendar year, so there is a delay of several months between the publishing of a year's numbers and the release of the respective year's Statistical Abstract.  
  
 Download the [2024 Statistical Abstract](https://irma.nps.gov/DataStore/DownloadFile/722329).  
  

## Data Limitations and Considerations

There are several ways to access Visitor Use Statistics data. Regardless of how you choose to access the data, it does have its limitations. Please read through the following list prior to using data ensure appropriate usage and interpretation.

#### Current Year Data Warning!

Current year data are preliminary and must be thoroughly reviewed by the Social Science Program prior to being considered final. For that reason, most data are available only through last calendar year.**If electing to use current year data, please use caution as it may not be complete or controlled for quality.**

#### Reporting Changes

The way visitor use statistics have been tracked and reported has changed over time. More information related to these shifts is available on the[History and Policy](https://www.nps.gov/subjects/socialscience/statistics-history.htm)page, but here is a quick guide to what data is available for different time periods:

*   **1904-1979**| Annual recreation visits
*   **1979-1992**| Annual and monthly values for the 11 official statistics
*   **1992-Present**| Same as previous with addition of park level data inputs used to calculate official statistics.

#### Count Procedure Changes

Parks change their methods for tracking and calculating visitor use stats from time to time. This can result in trend shift in the years following a change.

#### Varying degrees of data quality

Park operations and usage by visitors changes over time for most parks.**Updating counting methods can take a great deal of time and financial resources**for the park, making it challenging to keep measurement systems completely current and accurate.

**Parks also must sometimes rely on estimated data**due to equipment failures, staffing limitations, and unforeseeable circumstances such as the COVID-19 pandemic and natural disasters.

#### Rounding Difference

Depending on the data source, data users may notice slight rounding discrepancies across different reports.

#### Potential Errors

Once the calendar year is over and data for a given year is finalized, no changes to the underlying values can be made. Some parks' data may contain permanent errors.Errors are noted in the Endnotes of the[Annual Statistical Abstracts](https://irma.nps.gov/Stats/Reports/AbstractsAndForecasts).

NCCN North Coast and Cascades Network: National Park Service Inventory and Monitoring John R Boetsch National Park Service: North Coast and Cascades Network John_Boetsch@nps.gov https://orcid.org/0000-0003-0784-2211 Steve Acker National Park Service: Olympic National Park Issac A Quevedo National Park Service issac_quevedo@nps.gov https://orcid.org/0000-0003-0129-981X NCCN Christina Appleby National Park Service: North Coast and Cascades Network christina_appleby@partner.nps.gov https://orcid.org/0009-0009-3500-4881 metadata provider 2025-04-24 eng This data package contains North Coast and Cascades Network (NCCN) Inventory and Monitoring Program forest vegetation tabular data collected during 2005-2018 in Mount Rainier National Park (MORA), North Cascades National Park (NOCA), Olympic National Park (OLYM), and Lewis and Clark National Historical Park (LEWI).The protocol, publications, and all other associated links can be found in the project reference at: https://irma.nps.gov/DataStore/Reference/Profile/2182054.The diverse environmental conditions of th Pacific Northwest support various forest types, from coastal rainforests to subalpine fir forests, often containing mature forests that have not experienced recent stand-replacing disturbances. The North Coast and Cascades Network (NCCN) encompasses eight National Park Service units in the Pacific Northwest, with five parks featuring significant forest areas: Lewis and Clark National Historical Park (LEWI), Mount Rainier National Park (MORA), North Cascades National Park Service Complex (NOCA), Olympic National Park (OLYM), and San Juan Island National Historical Park (SAJH). Mature forests are integral to the character of these parks, and represent essential carbon stores and carbon sequestration potential. As such, forest vegetation has been identified as a key park ecosystem component in the development of NCCN's monitoring protocols.The primary objectives of the NCCN's forest monitoring program include tracking trends in tree recruitment, growth, mortality, and overall forest structure and composition, all as measures of forest health and integrity. Monitoring occurred in permanent one-hectare plots designed to align with the Forest Inventory and Analysis (FIA) program methodologies, incorporating a hierarchy of subplots for efficient data collection. These plots were designed to represent various forest types across the three large parks, focusing on warm-wet, cold-dry, and mid-elevation environments. Additionally, forests in the smaller parks were monitored with broader definitions of forest types. Specific parameters that were monitored include tree dimensions and health indicators, snag density and size, and environmental factors such as soil properties and landscape position. Complete measurements occurred every five years, while previously tagged trees were monitored annually for mortality to be able to detect short-term changes in tree condition.This comprehensive monitoring approach provides insights into the ecological dynamics of forest ecosystems, aiming to minimize the effects of succession while recognizing the significance of changing disturbance patterns (which have been monitored using remotely sensed imagery following a separate protocol, see https://irma.nps.gov/DataStore/Reference/Profile/2097545). This program aimed to detect subtle ecological changes, offering critical data for effective management of Pacific Northwest ecosystems amid ongoing environmental challenges.biology ecology monitoring http://www.nps.gov https://ror.org/044zqqy65 The protocol narrative describes the background, rationale, sampling design, field methods, analytical methods, data management, reporting, personnel requirements, and operational requirements for forest vegetation monitoring in LEWI, NOCA, MORA, and OLYM. Please refer to https://irma.nps.gov/DataStore/Reference/Profile/2164964 for the protocol narrative.Sampling Design The survey design for the NCCN's vegetation monitoring was structured to enhance ecological understanding and facilitate long-term monitoring of forest dynamics. It employed permanent one-hectare plots, conforming to standards set by the Forest Inventory and Analysis (FIA) program. This design intentionally prioritized static landscape characteristics, such as elevation, over dynamic community stratification, recognizing the ecological significance of such variables in influencing vegetation composition. By focusing on these characteristics, the survey aimed to capture changes in understory species and tree metrics effectively. Each plot was organized into a hierarchy of subplots, allowing for both intensive data collection and navigational efficiency in the often-challenging wilderness landscapes. This careful structuring not only ensured that the data collected were representative and reliable, but also maximized the safety and effectiveness of field crews operating in remote areas of the parks. Survey Methods The methods employed in the NCCN’s vegetation monitoring were grounded in the established protocols of the FIA, ensuring comparability and rigor in data collection. Trees within the plots were categorized into specific size classes — saplings (2.5 to 12.6 cm dbh), small trees (12.7 to 76.2 cm dbh), and large trees (> 76.2 cm dbh) — facilitating targeted assessments of forest composition and health. Comprehensive data collection involved not just basic measurements of species, height, and diameter at breast height, but also detailed observations of tree condition indicators, such as the presence of wildlife habitats, damage severity, and evidence of disease or mortality. Importantly, complete measurements of all tagged trees occurred every five years, while annual monitoring focused on previously recorded trees to note any mortality or significant changes in condition. This systematic approach allowed for a robust assessment of vegetation dynamics over time, providing critical insights into the health of forest ecosystems and informing future management strategies within the NCCN's parks.Data Management The data management cycle for NCCN involved a comprehensive process that included preparation, data acquisition, entry, quality review, metadata documentation, certification, delivery, analysis, product development, and archiving. Pre-season preparations focused on setting up project workspaces, ensuring GPS units were ready, and updating the project database, which was designed as a customized relational system using Microsoft SQL Server and Access. Data entry occurred immediately after field trips, with regular backups and verification processes to maintain accuracy. After certification, any edits to the data were tracked in an edit log, and a read-only copy of the certified data was retained for future reference.The data are certified. Data certification is a benchmark in the project information management process that indicates that: 1) the data are complete for the period of record; 2) they have undergone and passed the quality assurance checks; and 3) that they are appropriately documented and in a condition for archiving, posting and distribution as appropriate. Certification is not intended to imply that the data are completely free of errors or inconsistencies which may or may not have been detected during quality assurance reviews.Data Package Processing For the Plot Event Table, a Park_code column was added, date formatting was standardized to ISO 8601, and binary columns were converted from 1/0 to YES/NO before exporting as NCCN_Forests_Events.csv. The Plot Reference Table underwent similar date adjustments, included new columns with coordinate information, corrected Landform and Stratum descriptors, and renamed Elevation columns before being exported as NCCN_Forests_Locations.csv. The Tree Information Table incorporated scientific name resolution, formatting of the tree_type column, and unified value formatting, exporting as NCCN_Forests_TreeInformation.csv. Finally, the Tree Observations Table included key column adjustments while bringing in descriptors from lookup tables, adding units to column names, bringing in taxonomic information, and converting binary values, culminating in the export as NCCN_Forests_TreeObservations.csv. Missing values in character and categorical type columns were replaced with NULL, while missing values in date-time and numeric type columns were exported as 'blanks' in all The North Coast and Cascades Network (NCCN) encompasses eight National Park Service units in the Pacific Northwest, with five parks featuring significant forest areas: Lewis and Clark National Historical Park (LEWI), Mount Rainier National Park (MORA), North Cascades National Park Service Complex (NOCA), Olympic National Park (OLYM), and San Juan Island National Historical Park (SAJH). Mature forests are integral to the character of these parks, and represent essential carbon stores and carbon sequestration potential. As such, forest vegetation has been identified as a key park ecosystem component in the development of NCCN's monitoring protocols.The primary objectives of the NCCN's forest monitoring program include tracking trends in tree recruitment, growth, mortality, and overall forest structure and composition, all as measures of forest health and integrity. Monitoring occurred in permanent one-hectare plots designed to align with the Forest Inventory and Analysis (FIA) program methodologies, incorporating a hierarchy of subplots for efficient data collection. These plots were designed to represent various forest types across the three large parks, focusing on warm-wet, cold-dry, and mid-elevation environments. Additionally, forests in the smaller parks were monitored with broader definitions of forest types. Specific parameters that were monitored include tree dimensions and health indicators, snag density and size, and environmental factors such as soil properties and landscape position. Complete measurements occurred every five years, while previously tagged trees were monitored annually for mortality to be able to detect short-term changes in tree condition.This comprehensive monitoring approach provides insights into the ecological dynamics of forest ecosystems, aiming to minimize the effects of succession while recognizing the significance of changing disturbance patterns (which have been monitored using remotely sensed imagery following a separate protocol, see https://irma.nps.gov/DataStore/Reference/Profile/2097545). This program aimed to detect subtle ecological changes, offering critical data for effective management of Pacific Northwest ecosystems amid ongoing environmental challenges.biology ecology monitoring http://www.nps.gov https://ror.org/044zqqy65 The protocol narrative describes the background, rationale, sampling design, field methods, analytical methods, data management, reporting, personnel requirements, and operational requirements for forest vegetation monitoring in LEWI, NOCA, MORA, and OLYM. Please refer to https://irma.nps.gov/DataStore/Reference/Profile/2164964 for the protocol narrative.Sampling Design The survey design for the NCCN's vegetation monitoring was structured to enhance ecological understanding and facilitate long-term monitoring of forest dynamics. It employed permanent one-hectare plots, conforming to standards set by the Forest Inventory and Analysis (FIA) program. This design intentionally prioritized static landscape characteristics, such as elevation, over dynamic community stratification, recognizing the ecological significance of such variables in influencing vegetation composition. By focusing on these characteristics, the survey aimed to capture changes in understory species and tree metrics effectively. Each plot was organized into a hierarchy of subplots, allowing for both intensive data collection and navigational efficiency in the often-challenging wilderness landscapes. This careful structuring not only ensured that the data collected were representative and reliable, but also maximized the safety and effectiveness of field crews operating in remote areas of the parks. Survey Methods The methods employed in the NCCN’s vegetation monitoring were grounded in the established protocols of the FIA, ensuring comparability and rigor in data collection. Trees within the plots were categorized into specific size classes — saplings (2.5 to 12.6 cm dbh), small trees (12.7 to 76.2 cm dbh), and large trees (> 76.2 cm dbh) — facilitating targeted assessments of forest composition and health. Comprehensive data collection involved not just basic measurements of species, height, and diameter at breast height, but also detailed observations of tree condition indicators, such as the presence of wildlife habitats, damage severity, and evidence of disease or mortality. Importantly, complete measurements of all tagged trees occurred every five years, while annual monitoring focused on previously recorded trees to note any mortality or significant changes in condition. This systematic approach allowed for a robust assessment of vegetation dynamics over time, providing critical insights into the health of forest ecosystems and informing future management strategies within the NCCN's parks.Data Management The data management cycle for NCCN involved a comprehensive process that included preparation, data acquisition, entry, quality review, metadata documentation, certification, delivery, analysis, product development, and archiving. Pre-season preparations focused on setting up project workspaces, ensuring GPS units were ready, and updating the project database, which was designed as a customized relational system using Microsoft SQL Server and Access. Data entry occurred immediately after field trips, with regular backups and verification processes to maintain accuracy. After certification, any edits to the data were tracked in an edit log, and a read-only copy of the certified data was retained for future reference.The data are certified. Data certification is a benchmark in the project information management process that indicates that: 1) the data are complete for the period of record; 2) they have undergone and passed the quality assurance checks; and 3) that they are appropriately documented and in a condition for archiving, posting and distribution as appropriate. Certification is not intended to imply that the data are completely free of errors or inconsistencies which may or may not have been detected during quality assurance reviews.Data Package Processing For the Plot Event Table, a Park_code column was added, date formatting was standardized to ISO 8601, and binary columns were converted from 1/0 to YES/NO before exporting as NCCN_Forests_Events.csv. The Plot Reference Table underwent similar date adjustments, included new columns with coordinate information, corrected Landform and Stratum descriptors, and renamed Elevation columns before being exported as NCCN_Forests_Locations.csv. The Tree Information Table incorporated scientific name resolution, formatting of the tree_type column, and unified value formatting, exporting as NCCN_Forests_TreeInformation.csv. Finally, the Tree Observations Table included key column adjustments while bringing in descriptors from lookup tables, adding units to column names, bringing in taxonomic information, and converting binary values, culminating in the export as NCCN_Forests_TreeObservations.csv. Missing values in character and categorical type columns were replaced with NULL, while missing values in date-time and numeric type columns were exported as 'blanks' in all This booklet is intended for use by beginners in Alaska north of the Alaska Range. It includes 39 species descriptions, plus over 30 additional species noted in the ‘similar species’ sections. It will likely be a useful starting point for naturalists in Southwest and Southcentral Alaska, but the species selected and ‘similar species’ described are not tailored to those areas. We highly recommend those in Southeast Alaska look at resources for that region and the Pacific Northwest in the Additional Resources. Using a handlens (also called a loupe) or magnifying glass to look at lichens is highly recommended. This will bring you closer to the scale that these organisms live at, and help you see more details. Technical terms are underlined and defined in the glossary. Species included in the guide are bold and italicized , while species mentioned in comparison are simply italicized .Species are grouped by where they grow (ground, bark or rock) and then listed alphabetically by scientific name. We present common names for convenience, but these are not universally used. As this guide is intended for the curious but untrained beginner, we are attempting a balance between providing accurate information and making sure the language is clear. Some biological details have been simplified, and many rare species are not included in the potential look-alikes. If a specimen you are looking at doesn’t fit the descriptions, we encourage you to seek out more information. Inevitably, recognizing lichens takes practice. There is an incredible diversity of lichens in Alaska, and many species which have yet to be described by scientists. This guide presents just a glimpse into the most abundant part of the lichen flora in this region. Whether you live in Alaska or are passing through, we hope it encourages you to learn more about the ecology, biology and diversity of these unusual and underappreciated organisms.  

> Common Lichens of Northern Alaska 1

# ABOUT LICHENS 

What is a lichen? 

Lichens are symbiotic organisms . They are composed primarily of a mycobiont, a multi-celled fungus, and a photobiont, a photosynthetic partner, which is either a green algae or cyanobacteria. Other single-celled fungi and microorganisms likely play important roles in the symbiosis that are yet to be fully understood. Lichens (with some exceptions) have distinct layers where the symbionts occur (Fig 1). The upper layer, the cortex, is hard-packed fungal tissue, and is often shiny. It contains the multi-cellular mycobiont, single-celled yeasts and bacteria. Below that, the photobiont occurs in a single layer. Below that is another, looser layer made of fungal tissue, which allows for gas exchange. Some lichens have another cortex on the lower surface, some do not. Carefully breaking a lichen open with a fingernail can reveal these layers (look closely with a handlens).  

> Figure 1 .Lichen diagram. a: upper cortex, b: photobiont layer, c: medulla, d: lower cortex, e: rhizines.

About 20,000 species of lichen have been described by scientists. This represents about 20% of all known fungal species. And there are many more that have yet to be discovered. 

Are lichens parasitic? Do they hurt trees they grow on? No, lichens are not parasites ! Because they photosynthesize, lichens produce their own energy. They do not harm the trees they grow on. Lichens have a range of fungi that parasitize them, but they are not pathogenic. 

How fast do lichens grow? 

Very slowly ! The algae and cyanobacteria found in lichens can usually be cultured in test tubes and grow rapidly. The lichen-forming fungi, on the other hand, grow very sluggishly on petri dishes, if at all. Some scientists believe this is because coordinating growth between such different symbiotic partners is difficult. 

An alternative hypothesis is that their slow growth is a trade-off that lets them withstand environmental stress. Lichens can survive going from saturated with water to bone dry in seconds, which would kill most plants and animals. Instead of putting all the products from photosynthesis into growing bigger, lichens may create anti-desiccation compounds that protect their cells when they are dried out. This would necessarily mean that they can’t grow as fast as plants.  

> 2Common Lichens of Northern Alaska

Are lichens edible? 

Generally speaking, no, lichens are not edible . Because they are so slow-growing, lichens heavily invest in toxic chemical compounds that protect them from herbivores. Lichens are an important part of the winter diet of caribou, but these animals are specially adapted to eat lichens. Lichens are used in certain traditional foods by Alaska Natives and others, but these have to be carefully processed to remove the toxins. Unlike mushrooms, there are no lichens that are delicious edibles. Some lichens can be used for dyes and herbal medicine–but be careful! By collecting a lichen, you are killing the whole organism, which could be decades or hundreds of years old. No collection of lichens is allowed on National Park Service lands. Make sure you know where you’re collecting and be conscientious: collect an amount that won’t hurt the population, or other people’s enjoyment of wild spaces. 

Why are lichens such variable colors? 

One of the first things people notice is the variety of vivid yellows, reds, oranges, greens, blacks and browns found in lichens. These are a side effect the above-mentioned toxins in lichens–a variety of chemical compounds produced by the fungal partner. These chemical compounds protect the lichen from harmful UV radiation, deter herbivores and pathogens, help absorb toxic metals , and likely many more biological functions we don’t yet understand. While plants can protect themselves from UV and other stress by actively repairing their cells, lichens are exposed to the most stress when they are dried out and dormant. Thus, the protective compounds must be present all the time. Different colorful compounds can be helpful in different environments, or with different photobionts. Many lichens are a light mint or yellow green–this is not a result of the color of the algae! All the color you see when you look at a lichen is produced by the fungus, typically in the cortex or right above the photobiont layer. If a lichen does not have a cortex (true of the reindeer lichens and the undersurface of some species) it will usually be some shade of white–the natural color of the fungal tissue. Lichen fruiting bodies (apothecia, see page 7) are usually a different color than the rest of the lichen. It's likely that the photobiont needs different kinds of protection from environmental stress than the spore-producing apothecia, which are purely fungal tissue.  

> Common Lichens of Northern Alaska 3

Does stepping on lichens kill or injure them? 

It depends. Lichens can survive being broken–and in many species this is a way they spread. But fragmentation does reduce growth and it can take decades for them to recover. In general, try to avoid stepping on lichens when they are dry . If there’s a trail, stay on it. Walking over lichens enough times will kill them, and it’s best to limit the damage. 

All the same, Alaska is a large state and there are many lichen-rich areas that are inaccessible to people. Human hikers have far less impact on lichens than caribou, development, pollution, and climate shifts. 

Why are lichens only found in certain places? 

Because of their incredibly slow growth rates, lichens can only survive in places where they can’t be outshaded and outcompeted by fast-growing plants. They don’t have roots, but do have incredibly strong anchoring abilities, so they can grow in places where there is no soil. They can stay dormant for years if conditions are bad and then rapidly rehydrate and begin growing. They can also photosynthesize in sub-freezing temperatures. 

Lichens, then, are found in low-nutrient, high-stress environments: rock, tree bark, dead wood, and alpine and arctic tundra . Lichens make up such a large amount of the ground cover in Alaska and other high latitude locations because the cold, short growing season means they have a competitive edge against plants. (In the tropics, where many vines and other plants compete for space on tree trunks, some lichens are found on or even inside evergreen tree leaves.) 

Like all living organisms, lichens need water. They can get this in the form of precipitation, fog, or humidity. However, most lichens don’t photosynthesize well when waterlogged. Wet environments–like bogs and fens–tend to be dominated by mosses, primitive plants that thrive in high-moisture environments. 

Another factor that controls lichen distribution is air pollution. Lichens don’t have a waxy outer cuticle like our skin or plants–whatever chemicals are in the air, they directly absorb. This means they can’t survive in areas of high air pollution, like cities, around power plants, or other major industries. 

How are lichens important ecologically? 

Lichens are primary producers–they take energy from the sun and produce carbohydrates. They are at the base of the food chain and provide food for  

> 4Common Lichens of Northern Alaska

grazers (notably caribou) as well as decomposers when they die. Lichens also serve as habitat for invertebrates and other organisms. 

Lichens are also important for primary succession. They can grow on bare rock after volcanic eruptions, or glacial retreat exposes new ground. By growing on rock or sand, they build up organic matter and help create soil. 

Lichens that contain cyanobacteria are nitrogen-fixers. They can take atmospheric nitrogen and break its strong chemical bonds to produce nitrate. Nitrogen is an important nutrient that is used in all proteins, DNA, RNA and cell membranes. Lack of nitrogen in the soil often limits plant and animal growth, and lichens are important sources of nitrogen in boreal and arctic ecosystems. They are also important contributors to water and carbon cycling. 

For humans, lichens are used to monitor air pollution. Lichens are used in traditional herbal remedies and food in some cultures, and many lichen compounds are being studied for medicinal purposes. 

Lichens are part of the complex web of life, and more than being just ‘useful’ they are part of the rich natural heritage of our ecosystems. 

How can I tell lichens apart from mosses or other fungi? 

This can be tricky, because lichens have a wide range of body plans, anatomical structures and colors. Sometimes it's easiest to start out by pointing out what they don’t have. 

Unlike mosses, lichens do not have stems or leaves. To identify mosses, look for their simplified leaves attached to stems (Fig 2). Moss leaves are a single cell thick. Try to take them apart and hold a single leaf up to the light–it should be translucent.

Unlike other fungi, lichens do not have a mat of fungal hyphae embedded in the ground or wood. Lichens’ fruiting bodies last for many years–they don’t pop up for a few days and then rot, like mushrooms. One of the easiest ways to recognize a lichen vs a non-lichenized fungus is the texture. Lichens are tougher, and papery or brittle when dry. They are not slimy, mushy, gooey or otherwise easy to crumble. (There are a handful of mushroom-forming fungi that symbiotically associate with algae. These do have mushrooms, and don’t have the complex tissue layers that most lichens have.)

Identifying lichens takes practice. Compare what you see in this guide to mushroom hunting guides and other naturalist books. If you’re looking at a strange organism and stuck on what it could be, also consider non-lichenized fungi, liverworts, slime molds, rusts and plant galls. 

How can I recognize different species of lichen? (A brief intro to lichen anatomy) 

Lichens are commonly divided into three body plans (Figure 4). Note: these are not true evolutionary groups (like bats or birds), instead they are useful ways to talk about common features lichens share.  

> Figure 4. A crustose, foliose and fruticose lichen. Drawings © Lucy Taylor.
> 6Common Lichens of Northern Alaska

The first type of lichen is crustose (Fig 4a). This is the lichen body plan that evolved first, and 80% or more of all lichen species are crusts. Crustose lichens have an upper cortex, but are attached to the substrate like paint, and don’t have a distinct lower surface. The next body plan is foliose, or leaf-like (Fig 4b). These are lichens that are more or less two-dimensional– they have an upper and lower surface (or front and back). The third body plan is fruticose, or shrub-like. These lichens are essentially three-dimensional. They typically do not have a distinct front and back surface (Fig 4c). All lichens have a thallus, the vegetative body that contains photobionts. In addition, almost all lichen species also have some sort of reproductive structures (though many individuals you see will not). Lichens also reproduce by fragmentation. Three main reproductive structures are apothecia, isidia and soredia (Table 1, Figure 5).           

> Table 1.
> Structure Type Spreads Description
> Apothecia Sexual Only the fungi
> These cup, button, disk or dot-like structures are the fruiting body of the fungi (similar to a mushroom). They produce single-celled spores. They arise after sexual recombination, allowing for genetic diversity, but don’t disperse the photobiont.
> Isidia Asexual Whole symbiosis
> Outgrowths of the cortex that contain the photobiont. They can be many shapes–tiny cylinders or small globes are common. They contain the whole lichen and produce a clone of the parent. They are often shiny.
> Soredia Asexual Whole symbiosis
> Soredia are produced when the cortex disintegrates into a powder. This produces a fine dust that can be windborne and establish a new lichen. Like isidia, this is a clonal, whole-symbiosis form of reproduction.

Usually a species has only one type of reproductive structure (either apothecia, soredia or isidia). Apothecia are usually round in outline and a different color than the thallus (Fig 5a). The placement and shape of soredia or isidia can help identify the species. Some species have cephalodia (Fig 6a), which are pockets or freckles of cyanobacteria in a lichen which mainly contains green algae. (Such three-part lichens can rely on more productive green algae for the bulk of their photosynthesis, but also have the advantage of nitrogen fixation–they can be compared to hybrid cars.) Cephalodia come in a variety of shapes– freckles, spots, lumps or smudges–but are always dark, and distinct from the rest of the thallus. Other key characters include rhizines (root-like projections of the lower surface, fig 6b) and pseudocyphellae (openings in the cortex which expose the inner fungal tissue, fig 6c).

# GLOSSARY 

Apothecia – the fungal fruiting body, which produces single-celled spores. Typically more or less round in outline, it can be flat, concave or convex, and have a distinct rim or not. Spores are contained in a structure called an ‘ascus,’ which shoots them into the air. Cephalodia – A ‘pocket’ of fungal tissue which contains cyanobacteria on a lichen that has green algae as its main photobiont. Cephalodia are dark in color. Cortex – An outer layer of densely packed fungal tissue. Contains other symbiotic partners, such as single-celled yeasts, and often contains secondary chemicals and pigments. Crustose – A lichen that is closely appressed to the substrate, like paint, without a lower cortex. Cannot be removed from the substrate without destroying the lichen. Cyanobacteria – single-celled or filamentous bacteria that are capable of photosynthesis as well as nitrogen-fixation. Cyanobacteria are not as productive photosynthesizers as green algae, and need liquid water and light in order to fix nitrogen. The most common cyanobacteria photobiont are members of the genus Nostoc , which can also live independently. Genus – group of closely related species. For example, horses and zebras are in the same genus. The genus name is the first part of any scientific name: the deadman’s finger lichen Dactylina arctica is in the genus 

Dactylina .Green algae – single-celled photosynthetic eukaryotic organisms. The evolutionary ancestor of all land plants. Many green algae found as lichen photobionts are also found free-living, growing on bark or rocks. Foliose – leaf-like lichens. Have an upper and lower surface (or front and back side). Fruticose – shrub-like lichens. Similar from multiple angles (but often have a top and bottom). Isidia – projections of the cortex which contain both mycobiont and photobiont. Can be various shapes; commonly cylinders or globes. Disperses the lichen clonally. Macrolichen – an informal group that includes fruticose and foliose lichens and excludes crusts.  

> Common Lichens of Northern Alaska 9

Medulla – the largest layer in a lichen thallus, located below the photobiont layer. Made up of loosely packed fungal tissue. Usually white, sometimes yellow. Moss – early land plants with single-cell thick leaves and no roots or vascular tissues. Grow in similar habitats as lichens to similar sizes, and are also able to tolerate desiccation. Mycobiont – the multicellular fungal partner of the lichen symbiosis. Almost always an ascomycete fungus (cup-forming fungus). Peltate – attached at a central point, like a mushroom or umbrella. Photobiont – the single-celled photosynthetic partner of the symbiosis. Either green algae or cyanobacteria. Some lichens have both (see: cephalodia). Pseudocyphellae – an opening in the cortex which exposes the lower fungal layers (medulla). Allows for gas exchange. Rhizine – a projection of the lower surface into a root or hair-like structure. Sometimes branched. Found exclusively on foliose lichens. Helps anchor the lichen to its substrate, allow air flow beneath the lichen, and increases surface area for water absorption. Soredia – a disintegration of the cortex into a dust-like powder. Contains all symbiotic partners. They are spread by wind. Disperses the lichen clonally. Squamule – small scale-like pieces of the thallus, with an upper cortex. Lichens can have squamules attached to stem-like structures (particularly in Cladonia and Stereocaulon ), or the whole thallus can be made up of squamules. Thallus – the body of the lichen. Contains all partners of the symbiosis and carries out vegetation growth. Can come in many different shapes. Vascular plants – what are commonly thought of as plants. Examples include horsetails, ferns, pine trees and daisies. Have true leaves and roots, and stems with cells specialized for water transport (vascular tissue). Veins – raised, often branching, ridges of tissue. Commonly found on the underside of Peltigera .

Lichens of North America by Irwin Brodo, Sylvia Duran Sharnoff & Stephen Sharnoff: A large coffee table book, it has great introductory material on lichens, keys, beautiful color photos, and descriptions of hundreds of lichens from across the continent. 

Other beginner resources for Alaskans 

Common Cryptogams of Interior Alaska by Gary A. Laursen & Rodney Seppelt: Color guidebook, includes mushrooms, lichens, mosses and liverworts. Includes 12 lichens and more technical detail than this guide. Lichens Around Mendenhall Glacier by Chiska C. Derr & Robert Hasselbach: great introductory resource for Southeast Alaska. Lichens of Alaska’s South Coast by Karen Dillman: Forest Service brochure, includes 31 lichens common to SE Alaska. 

Technical books and keys useful for Alaska 

Compendium of Lichens and Associated Fungi of Alaska: List of all lichens reported in the scientific literature for Alaska. A good resource for checking a species reported range, but does not come with keys. Free PDF available online. Lichens of British Columbia, Volume 1 and Volume 2 by Trevor Goward: Illustrated keys, often include Alaskan species. PDFs available free online. Macrolichens of the Pacific Northwest by Bruce McCune and Linda Geiser: Paperback book with keys, descriptions & photos. Microlichens of the Pacific Northwest, Volumes 1 & 2. by Bruce McCune: Keys, photos, and descriptions of crustose lichens. Volume 1 has a superb illustrated glossary. Keys to the Lichens of North America by Irwin Brodo: One of the most complete keys available. No photos. 

Websites 

The British Lichen Society : resources for chemical spot tests and a more complete glossary of anatomical terms. Ways of Enlichenment: Includes writing about lichens, and one of the best lichen photo galleries available online, with all IDs verified by experts. Based in British Columbia. iNaturalist: A website for uploading and identifying species observations. Good source of photos and locations of many lichens, and feedback on your IDs, but remember: many species cannot be identified from photos. IDs are often incorrect. This booklet is intended for use by beginners in Alaska north of the Alaska Range. It includes 39 species descriptions, plus over 30 additional species noted in the ‘similar species’ sections. It will likely be a useful starting point for naturalists in Southwest and Southcentral Alaska, but the species selected and ‘similar species’ described are not tailored to those areas. We highly recommend those in Southeast Alaska look at resources for that region and the Pacific Northwest in the Additional Resources. Using a handlens (also called a loupe) or magnifying glass to look at lichens is highly recommended. This will bring you closer to the scale that these organisms live at, and help you see more details. Technical terms are underlined and defined in the glossary. Species included in the guide are bold and italicized , while species mentioned in comparison are simply italicized .Species are grouped by where they grow (ground, bark or rock) and then listed alphabetically by scientific name. We present common names for convenience, but these are not universally used. As this guide is intended for the curious but untrained beginner, we are attempting a balance between providing accurate information and making sure the language is clear. Some biological details have been simplified, and many rare species are not included in the potential look-alikes. If a specimen you are looking at doesn’t fit the descriptions, we encourage you to seek out more information. Inevitably, recognizing lichens takes practice. There is an incredible diversity of lichens in Alaska, and many species which have yet to be described by scientists. This guide presents just a glimpse into the most abundant part of the lichen flora in this region. Whether you live in Alaska or are passing through, we hope it encourages you to learn more about the ecology, biology and diversity of these unusual and underappreciated organisms.

# ABOUT LICHENS 

What is a lichen? 

Lichens are symbiotic organisms . They are composed primarily of a mycobiont, a multi-celled fungus, and a photobiont, a photosynthetic partner, which is either a green algae or cyanobacteria. Other single-celled fungi and microorganisms likely play important roles in the symbiosis that are yet to be fully understood. Lichens (with some exceptions) have distinct layers where the symbionts occur (Fig 1). The upper layer, the cortex, is hard-packed fungal tissue, and is often shiny. It contains the multi-cellular mycobiont, single-celled yeasts and bacteria. Below that, the photobiont occurs in a single layer. Below that is another, looser layer made of fungal tissue, which allows for gas exchange. Some lichens have another cortex on the lower surface, some do not. Carefully breaking a lichen open with a fingernail can reveal these layers (look closely with a handlens).  

> Figure 1 .Lichen diagram. a: upper cortex, b: photobiont layer, c: medulla, d: lower cortex, e: rhizines.

About 20,000 species of lichen have been described by scientists. This represents about 20% of all known fungal species. And there are many more that have yet to be discovered. 

Are lichens parasitic? Do they hurt trees they grow on? No, lichens are not parasites ! Because they photosynthesize, lichens produce their own energy. They do not harm the trees they grow on. Lichens have a range of fungi that parasitize them, but they are not pathogenic. 

How fast do lichens grow? 

Very slowly ! The algae and cyanobacteria found in lichens can usually be cultured in test tubes and grow rapidly. The lichen-forming fungi, on the other hand, grow very sluggishly on petri dishes, if at all. Some scientists believe this is because coordinating growth between such different symbiotic partners is difficult. 

An alternative hypothesis is that their slow growth is a trade-off that lets them withstand environmental stress. Lichens can survive going from saturated with water to bone dry in seconds, which would kill most plants and animals. Instead of putting all the products from photosynthesis into growing bigger, lichens may create anti-desiccation compounds that protect their cells when they are dried out. This would necessarily mean that they can’t grow as fast as plants.  

> 2Common Lichens of Northern Alaska

Are lichens edible? 

Generally speaking, no, lichens are not edible . Because they are so slow-growing, lichens heavily invest in toxic chemical compounds that protect them from herbivores. Lichens are an important part of the winter diet of caribou, but these animals are specially adapted to eat lichens. Lichens are used in certain traditional foods by Alaska Natives and others, but these have to be carefully processed to remove the toxins. Unlike mushrooms, there are no lichens that are delicious edibles. Some lichens can be used for dyes and herbal medicine–but be careful! By collecting a lichen, you are killing the whole organism, which could be decades or hundreds of years old. No collection of lichens is allowed on National Park Service lands. Make sure you know where you’re collecting and be conscientious: collect an amount that won’t hurt the population, or other people’s enjoyment of wild spaces. 

Why are lichens such variable colors? 

One of the first things people notice is the variety of vivid yellows, reds, oranges, greens, blacks and browns found in lichens. These are a side effect the above-mentioned toxins in lichens–a variety of chemical compounds produced by the fungal partner. These chemical compounds protect the lichen from harmful UV radiation, deter herbivores and pathogens, help absorb toxic metals , and likely many more biological functions we don’t yet understand. While plants can protect themselves from UV and other stress by actively repairing their cells, lichens are exposed to the most stress when they are dried out and dormant. Thus, the protective compounds must be present all the time. Different colorful compounds can be helpful in different environments, or with different photobionts. Many lichens are a light mint or yellow green–this is not a result of the color of the algae! All the color you see when you look at a lichen is produced by the fungus, typically in the cortex or right above the photobiont layer. If a lichen does not have a cortex (true of the reindeer lichens and the undersurface of some species) it will usually be some shade of white–the natural color of the fungal tissue. Lichen fruiting bodies (apothecia, see page 7) are usually a different color than the rest of the lichen. It's likely that the photobiont needs different kinds of protection from environmental stress than the spore-producing apothecia, which are purely fungal tissue.  

> Common Lichens of Northern Alaska 3

Does stepping on lichens kill or injure them? 

It depends. Lichens can survive being broken–and in many species this is a way they spread. But fragmentation does reduce growth and it can take decades for them to recover. In general, try to avoid stepping on lichens when they are dry . If there’s a trail, stay on it. Walking over lichens enough times will kill them, and it’s best to limit the damage. 

All the same, Alaska is a large state and there are many lichen-rich areas that are inaccessible to people. Human hikers have far less impact on lichens than caribou, development, pollution, and climate shifts. 

Why are lichens only found in certain places? 

Because of their incredibly slow growth rates, lichens can only survive in places where they can’t be outshaded and outcompeted by fast-growing plants. They don’t have roots, but do have incredibly strong anchoring abilities, so they can grow in places where there is no soil. They can stay dormant for years if conditions are bad and then rapidly rehydrate and begin growing. They can also photosynthesize in sub-freezing temperatures. 

Lichens, then, are found in low-nutrient, high-stress environments: rock, tree bark, dead wood, and alpine and arctic tundra . Lichens make up such a large amount of the ground cover in Alaska and other high latitude locations because the cold, short growing season means they have a competitive edge against plants. (In the tropics, where many vines and other plants compete for space on tree trunks, some lichens are found on or even inside evergreen tree leaves.) 

Like all living organisms, lichens need water. They can get this in the form of precipitation, fog, or humidity. However, most lichens don’t photosynthesize well when waterlogged. Wet environments–like bogs and fens–tend to be dominated by mosses, primitive plants that thrive in high-moisture environments. 

Another factor that controls lichen distribution is air pollution. Lichens don’t have a waxy outer cuticle like our skin or plants–whatever chemicals are in the air, they directly absorb. This means they can’t survive in areas of high air pollution, like cities, around power plants, or other major industries. 

How are lichens important ecologically? 

Lichens are primary producers–they take energy from the sun and produce carbohydrates. They are at the base of the food chain and provide food for  

> 4Common Lichens of Northern Alaska

grazers (notably caribou) as well as decomposers when they die. Lichens also serve as habitat for invertebrates and other organisms. 

Lichens are also important for primary succession. They can grow on bare rock after volcanic eruptions, or glacial retreat exposes new ground. By growing on rock or sand, they build up organic matter and help create soil. 

Lichens that contain cyanobacteria are nitrogen-fixers. They can take atmospheric nitrogen and break its strong chemical bonds to produce nitrate. Nitrogen is an important nutrient that is used in all proteins, DNA, RNA and cell membranes. Lack of nitrogen in the soil often limits plant and animal growth, and lichens are important sources of nitrogen in boreal and arctic ecosystems. They are also important contributors to water and carbon cycling. 

For humans, lichens are used to monitor air pollution. Lichens are used in traditional herbal remedies and food in some cultures, and many lichen compounds are being studied for medicinal purposes. 

Lichens are part of the complex web of life, and more than being just ‘useful’ they are part of the rich natural heritage of our ecosystems. 

How can I tell lichens apart from mosses or other fungi? 

This can be tricky, because lichens have a wide range of body plans, anatomical structures and colors. Sometimes it's easiest to start out by pointing out what they don’t have. 

Unlike mosses, lichens do not have stems or leaves. To identify mosses, look for their simplified leaves attached to stems (Fig 2). Moss leaves are a single cell thick. Try to take them apart and hold a single leaf up to the light–it should be translucent. 

> Figure 2. A single moss plant, with tiny, translucent leaves. (Fingertips for scale.)

# leaves  

> Common Lichens of Northern Alaska 5

Unlike other fungi, lichens do not have a mat of fungal hyphae embedded in the ground or wood. Lichens’ fruiting bodies last for many years–they don’t pop up for a few days and then rot, like mushrooms. One of the easiest ways to recognize a lichen vs a non-lichenized fungus is the texture. Lichens are tougher, and papery or brittle when dry. They are not slimy, mushy, gooey or otherwise easy to crumble. (There are a handful of mushroom-forming fungi that symbiotically associate with algae. These do have mushrooms, and don’t have the complex tissue layers that most lichens have.)    

> Figure 3. Some organisms that are not lichens: Free-living cyanobacteria ( Nostoc commune ), free-living green algae on a birch tree ( Trentepohlia sp., photo CC BY-NC Michał S.), common liverwort ( Marchantia polymorpha ), rosy goblet ( Microstoma protractum , non-lichenized fungi).

Identifying lichens takes practice. Compare what you see in this guide to mushroom hunting guides and other naturalist books. If you’re looking at a strange organism and stuck on what it could be, also consider non-lichenized fungi, liverworts, slime molds, rusts and plant galls. 

How can I recognize different species of lichen? (A brief intro to lichen anatomy) 

Lichens are commonly divided into three body plans (Figure 4). Note: these are not true evolutionary groups (like bats or birds), instead they are useful ways to talk about common features lichens share.  

> Figure 4. A crustose, foliose and fruticose lichen. Drawings © Lucy Taylor.
> 6Common Lichens of Northern Alaska

The first type of lichen is crustose (Fig 4a). This is the lichen body plan that evolved first, and 80% or more of all lichen species are crusts. Crustose lichens have an upper cortex, but are attached to the substrate like paint, and don’t have a distinct lower surface. The next body plan is foliose, or leaf-like (Fig 4b). These are lichens that are more or less two-dimensional– they have an upper and lower surface (or front and back). The third body plan is fruticose, or shrub-like. These lichens are essentially three-dimensional. They typically do not have a distinct front and back surface (Fig 4c). All lichens have a thallus, the vegetative body that contains photobionts. In addition, almost all lichen species also have some sort of reproductive structures (though many individuals you see will not). Lichens also reproduce by fragmentation. Three main reproductive structures are apothecia, isidia and soredia (Table 1, Figure 5).           

> Table 1.
> Structure Type Spreads Description
> Apothecia Sexual Only the fungi
> These cup, button, disk or dot-like structures are the fruiting body of the fungi (similar to a mushroom). They produce single-celled spores. They arise after sexual recombination, allowing for genetic diversity, but don’t disperse the photobiont.
> Isidia Asexual Whole symbiosis
> Outgrowths of the cortex that contain the photobiont. They can be many shapes–tiny cylinders or small globes are common. They contain the whole lichen and produce a clone of the parent. They are often shiny.

> Soredia are produced when the cortex disintegrates into a powder. This produces a fine dust that can be windborne and establish a new lichen. Like isidia, this is a clonal, whole-symbiosis form of reproduction.

Usually a species has only one type of reproductive structure (either apothecia, soredia or isidia). Apothecia are usually round in outline and a different color than the thallus (Fig 5a). The placement and shape of soredia or isidia can help identify the species. Some species have cephalodia (Fig 6a), which are pockets or freckles of cyanobacteria in a lichen which mainly contains green algae. (Such three-part lichens can rely on more productive green algae for the bulk of their photosynthesis, but also have the advantage of nitrogen fixation–they can be compared to hybrid cars.) Cephalodia come in a variety of shapes– freckles, spots, lumps or smudges–but are always dark, and distinct from the rest of the thallus. Other key characters include rhizines (root-like projections of the lower surface, fig 6b) and pseudocyphellae (openings in the cortex which expose the inner fungal tissue, fig 6c).

# GLOSSARY 

Apothecia – the fungal fruiting body, which produces single-celled spores. Typically more or less round in outline, it can be flat, concave or convex, and have a distinct rim or not. Spores are contained in a structure called an ‘ascus,’ which shoots them into the air. Cephalodia – A ‘pocket’ of fungal tissue which contains cyanobacteria on a lichen that has green algae as its main photobiont. Cephalodia are dark in color. Cortex – An outer layer of densely packed fungal tissue. Contains other symbiotic partners, such as single-celled yeasts, and often contains secondary chemicals and pigments. Crustose – A lichen that is closely appressed to the substrate, like paint, without a lower cortex. Cannot be removed from the substrate without destroying the lichen. Cyanobacteria – single-celled or filamentous bacteria that are capable of photosynthesis as well as nitrogen-fixation. Cyanobacteria are not as productive photosynthesizers as green algae, and need liquid water and light in order to fix nitrogen. The most common cyanobacteria photobiont are members of the genus Nostoc , which can also live independently. Genus – group of closely related species. For example, horses and zebras are in the same genus. The genus name is the first part of any scientific name: the deadman’s finger lichen Dactylina arctica is in the genus 

Dactylina .Green algae – single-celled photosynthetic eukaryotic organisms. The evolutionary ancestor of all land plants. Many green algae found as lichen photobionts are also found free-living, growing on bark or rocks. Foliose – leaf-like lichens. Have an upper and lower surface (or front and back side). Fruticose – shrub-like lichens. Similar from multiple angles (but often have a top and bottom). Isidia – projections of the cortex which contain both mycobiont and photobiont. Can be various shapes; commonly cylinders or globes. Disperses the lichen clonally. Macrolichen – an informal group that includes fruticose and foliose lichens and excludes crusts.  

> Common Lichens of Northern Alaska 9

Medulla – the largest layer in a lichen thallus, located below the photobiont layer. Made up of loosely packed fungal tissue. Usually white, sometimes yellow. Moss – early land plants with single-cell thick leaves and no roots or vascular tissues. Grow in similar habitats as lichens to similar sizes, and are also able to tolerate desiccation. Mycobiont – the multicellular fungal partner of the lichen symbiosis. Almost always an ascomycete fungus (cup-forming fungus). Peltate – attached at a central point, like a mushroom or umbrella. Photobiont – the single-celled photosynthetic partner of the symbiosis. Either green algae or cyanobacteria. Some lichens have both (see: cephalodia). Pseudocyphellae – an opening in the cortex which exposes the lower fungal layers (medulla). Allows for gas exchange. Rhizine – a projection of the lower surface into a root or hair-like structure. Sometimes branched. Found exclusively on foliose lichens. Helps anchor the lichen to its substrate, allow air flow beneath the lichen, and increases surface area for water absorption. Soredia – a disintegration of the cortex into a dust-like powder. Contains all symbiotic partners. They are spread by wind. Disperses the lichen clonally. Squamule – small scale-like pieces of the thallus, with an upper cortex. Lichens can have squamules attached to stem-like structures (particularly in Cladonia and Stereocaulon ), or the whole thallus can be made up of squamules. Thallus – the body of the lichen. Contains all partners of the symbiosis and carries out vegetation growth. Can come in many different shapes. Vascular plants – what are commonly thought of as plants. Examples include horsetails, ferns, pine trees and daisies. Have true leaves and roots, and stems with cells specialized for water transport (vascular tissue). Veins – raised, often branching, ridges of tissue. Commonly found on the underside of Peltigera .
