Green witch’s hair lichen  

> Alectoria ochroleuca – fruticose

Description: This hair lichen is much-branched and grows on rock and the ground in the tundra. It is mainly yellow, and the tips can turn dark green. It has regular raised, oval bumps the same color as the thallus (look with a handlens). 

Similar species: Grey witch’s hair (Alectoria nigricans ) has similar branching and bumps, but it is pinkish to grey at the base and black at the tips. 

Heath foxhair lichen  

> Bryocaulon divergens – fruticose

Description: This hair lichen often forms dense mats in tundra. Its color is orange or chestnut brown if in the shade, to black-brown in full sun. It has prominent white pseudocyphellae (look with a handlens). 

Similar species: Tundra horsehair lichen 

(Bryoria nitidula ) is a similar dark hair lichen but does not have the white patches. The genus Pseudephebe grows closely attached to rock and with much smaller branches (~.1 mm wide). 

Arctic rag lichen  

> Asahinea chrysantha – foliose

Description: Found in arctic and alpine tundra across Alaska, typically over rocks or on the ground. The lobes are rounded. It has a net-ridged, light yellow upper surface and a brown to black smooth undersurface. 

Similar species: Crinkled snow lichen (Flavocetraria nivalis , page 16) has a yellow undersurface. Scholander’s rag lichen ( Asahinea scholanderi ) grows closely appressed to rock and has isidia over the upper surface.  

> 12 Common Lichens of Northern Alaska

Striped iceland lichen 

Cetraria laevigata – foliose 

Description: Found in tundra, bogs, and shrubby habitats. Grows semi-upright. It has small spines along the edges, and near-continuous white pseudocyphellae near the edge of the thallus. In full sun it is brown, shaded it is tan to green. 

Similar species: Iceland lichen ( Cetraria islandica ) is similar, but has white pseudocyphellae pock-marked along the back, not just the edge. Alaska has several other brown Cetraria species; see the keys in 

Additional Resources .

Pixie lichens 

Cladonia species – fruticose (Pictured: Cladonia chlorophaea )

Description: Pixie lichens are a large and variable genus, with ~90 species in Alaska. They are usually yellow, green or brown. Key features to distinguish different species include: a yellow cast, the presence of cups, soredia, apothecia (and the color of the apothecia), branching patterns, basal squamules, and chemical tests. 

Similar species: These are the only lichens that form cups on stalks. Many species also grow over logs or trees. 

Quill lichen 

Cladonia amaurocraea – fruticose 

Description: Quill lichen is a widespread, highly variable pixie cup lichen. It grows in bogs and tundra. It has a distinct yellow-green color with brown tips. Its shape is highly variable: it can be unbranched (forming long points, typically found in bogs), much-branched, or branched and cupped. 

Similar species: Thorn lichen ( Cladonia uncialis ) is thicker with larger holes in the axils, a lighter yellow, & never forms cups or long points. 

Common Lichens of Northern Alaska 13 

ON THE GROUND Yellow reindeer lichen  

> Cladonia arbuscula – fruticose

Description: This species is much-branched, lacks a hard cortex and is pale yellow. It is an important part of caribou’s winter diet. It is found in woodlands and the tundra.    

> Similar species: Grey reindeer lichen (Cladonia rangiferina ,below) is also much branched, but lacks the light yellow cast and has a ‘wind-swept’ appearance. It helps to hold two specimens side by side to see the difference in color. See also Cladonia stellaris , facing.

Boreal cup lichen  

> Cladonia borealis – fruticose

Description: This is one of our most common red-fruited lichens. It has small squamules on the podetia. It glows blue under UV light. 

Similar species: There are several other species of pixie lichen ( Cladonia ) in Alaska, some of which have red apothecia. Note: British soldier lichen (Cladonia cristatella ) is an eastern species that does not occur in the state. 

Grey reindeer lichen  

> Cladonia rangiferina – fruticose

Description: Grey reindeer lichen is much-branched, and typically has a ‘wind-swept’ appearance, with branch tips bent one direction. It lacks a yellow cast and turns brown at the base. It is found in woodlands and the tundra. 

Similar species: Black-footed reindeer lichen ( Cladonia stygia ) is just as common as grey reindeer lichen in northern Alaska. It blackens at the base. See also yellow reindeer lichen, above.  

> 14 Common Lichens of Northern Alaska

ON THE GROUND Star-tipped reindeer lichen  

> Cladonia stellaris – fruticose

Description: Like the other reindeer lichens, this species is much-branched and lacks an outer cortex. It is distinguished by the dense branching, which forms even, round, ‘puffball’-like heads. It is also found in a variety of woodland, heath and tundra habitats. It is pale yellow in color. 

Similar species: See the entries for yellow and grey reindeer lichens (facing). 

Dead man’s fingers   

> Dactylina arctica –fruticose

Description: Typically found growing upright in the tundra, dead man’s fingers is a knobbly lichen, yellow to tan in color. It is unbranched or occasionally branched. If broken open it is hollow with cobwebby tendrils inside. 

Similar species: Whiteworm lichen (Thamnolia vermicularis , pg 19) is a similar shape, but pure white. The related frosted finger lichen ( Dactylina ramulosa ) is much-branched with a thorny appearance and has a white-purple cast. 

Curled snow lichen  

> Flavocetraria cucullata – foliose

Description: Found in bogs and tundra, growing over mosses or on the ground. It is widespread across the boreal zone. The lobes are yellow, narrow, and inrolled, often fusing into a tube. 

Similar species: Crinkled snow lichen (Flavocetraria nivalis , pg 16) has a similar color, but a net-ridged texture, not inrolled lobes. The rare Flavocetraria miniscula is much smaller (2-3 cm) and has helmet-shaped hooked tips.  

> Common Lichens of Northern Alaska 15

ON THE GROUND Crinkled snow lichen  

> Flavocetraria nivalis – foliose

Description: Crinkled snow lichen is found on tundra, often in late-lying snow areas, growing on the ground. It is widespread across the boreal zone. The lobes are broad, loosely branched, with a net-ridged texture across the thallus. 

Similar species: Crinkled snow lichen is the only tundra-growing species that is net-ridged and light yellow on both sides. 

Pink fairy barf  

> Icmadophila ericetorum – crustose

Description: This lichen grows over moss mats (particularly peat moss, 

Sphagnum ) or sometimes logs and tree bases. It is a crustose lichen. The thallus is mint green and warty. The pink apothecia do not have rims. 

Similar species: There are several other green crustose lichens, but none of them have pink, rimless apothecia. 

Cabbage lung  

> Lobaria linita – foliose

Description: Grows over mossy rocks in the tundra and sometimes tree bases. Lime green to gold when wet and dull gray-green when dry. It has a prominent pattern of ridges and hollows. The underside is pale, with short brown hairs in the ridges. 

Similar species: The lung lichens (Lobaria ) are distinguished from other green foliose lichens by the pattern of ridges. Several species of lung lichen are common on trees, particularly in southern Alaska.  

> 16 Common Lichens of Northern Alaska

ON THE GROUND Tumbleweed lichen 

Masonhalea richardsonii – foliose 

Description: This is one of the largest and most distinctive lichens in Alaska. It is found in swales in the tundra. When dry, it curls up into a ball and is easily carried by the wind. When wet, it spreads out. It is dark brown, branched, and with long white patches on the outer surface (pseudocyphellae). 

Similar species: Tumbleweed lichen looks similar to some brown species of Cetraria ,but it is the only lichen in Alaska that grows loose in the tundra. 

Arctic kidney lichen 

Nephroma arcticum – foliose 

Description: Arctic kidney lichen grows in rounded lobes in the tundra. It is pale yellow green when dry and a more vibrant mint green when wet. It is tan on the underside, darkening to the base. In the center, you can sometimes see dark blue patches (cephalodia) which contain cyanobacteria. Apothecia, when present, are large orange-tan discs. 

Similar species: Alpine kidney lichen (Nephroma expallidum ) is smaller, more ruffled, and browner. The tree-dwelling species of kidney lichen are brown. 

Freckle pelt 

Peltigera aphthosa – foliose 

Description: Alaska has three common freckle pelt lichens, found in the boreal forest and tundra. They all have veins and rhizines on the underside, are grass green when wet (grayish when dry), and have black cephalodia ‘freckles’ over the upper surface. In Peltigera aphthosa (pictured), the cephalodia are closely attached to the surface, and the edges aren’t ruffled. 

Similar species: Peltigera leucophlebi a has strongly ruffled lobes. P. britannica , found south of the AK Range, has peltate cephalodia. Other species of Peltigera have veins & rhizines below, but no cephalodia. 

Common Lichens of Northern Alaska 17 

ON THE GROUND Dog pelt  

> Peltigera canina – foliose

Description: A large grey lichen, often found in dry or disturbed environments. The upper side often has a white mat of hairs, particularly towards the lobe tips. The rhizines on the undersurface are densely tufted.    

> Similar species: There are many grey species of Peltigera , distinguished by reproductive structures, vein patterns and the rhizines. The large size (lobes 2-4 cm across), downturned lobe tips, and bottlebrush rhizines are distinctive. Compare: P. membranacea , pg 8.

Globe lichen  

> Sphaerophorus globosus – fruticose

Description: This small lichen is found in the alpine, growing mixed with other lichens & mosses. The color is a rich orange. The branches are round in cross-section and not hollow.    

> Similar species: Fragile coral lichen (Sphaerophorus fragilis ) is greyer, less branched, and the side branches the same size as the main branch. That species is typically found directly on rock. There are two species of Sphaerophorus in southern Alaska which grow on trees.

Chocolate chip lichen  

> Solorina crocea – foliose

Description: Chocolate chip lichen grows in rosettes on mineral soil in the tundra. It is bright green, with inset brown ‘chocolate chip’ apothecia. The underside is vivid orange. 

Similar species: This is the only green lichen with an orange undersurface in Alaska. Similar lichens include pelt lichens (particularly Peltigera venosa ) and other members of the genus Solorina ,which also have sunken apothecia.  

> 18 Common Lichens of Northern Alaska

ON THE GROUND Foam lichens 

Stereocaulon species – fruticose 

Description: The round stems are pale pink, and support many grey, shingle-like squamules. Sometimes they have brown apothecia or dark cephalodia. Found in a variety of habitats, including woodlands, tundra, and rocky or sandy riverbanks, foam lichens are vital pioneer species. 

Similar species: The white crustose lichens 

Ochrolechia frigida and Lepra dactylina can look similar. Devil’s matchstick ( Pilophorus 

spp.) is also grey, but is topped by black apothecia. 

Whiteworm lichen 

Thamnolia vermicularis – fruticose 

Description: This species is found in tundra. It is pure white, pointed, unbranched or irregularly branched, and hollow on the inside. Unusually, it is exclusively clonal, and spreads solely through fragmentation. 

Similar species: This is the only pure white, hollow lichen in Alaska. The uncommon waterfingers ( Siphula ceratites ) is also white and finger-like, but it grows in wet places (often in standing water), has blunt tips, and is solid. 

Yellow lichen 

Vulpicida juniperinus – foliose 

Description: The name describes its most noticeable feature: a vivid saffron orange color. It grows in round clusters on rocky soil. 

Similar species: The closely related powdered sunshine lichen ( Vulpicida pinastri , page 21) grows on bark, and has bright yellow soredia along the edge. There are several paler yellow foliose lichens: see 

Asahinea chrysantha , Flavocetraria cucullata and Flavocetraria nivalis .

Common Lichens of Northern Alaska 19 

ON THE GROUND Boreal oakmoss   

> Evernia mesomorpha –fruticose

Description: One of the most common lichens in the boreal forest. The thallus is mint green, and becomes covered with soredia as it ages. It is solid and white on the inside, without a stretchy central strand. It is usually evenly branched, lumpy and irregular if parasitized.  

> Similar species: Bushy lichens ( Ramalina
> species) are a similar color, but +/- hollow, and not covered in soredia. Also see old man’s beard ( Usnea , facing).

Hooded tube lichen  

> Hypogymnia physodes – foliose

Description: This lichen is light grey to greenish above, black below, and hollow. It can grow in a rosette or hang from twigs, bark and wood. In mature individuals, the tips flare open and display patches of powdery soredia inside (look with a handlens).    

> Similar species: There are several other species of tube lichen in northern Alaska. They are typically brown ( Hypogymnia bitteri
> and H. austerodes ) and do not flare open at the tip. Some species grow on tundra (common: H. subobscura ).

Bearded jellyskin  

> Leptogium saturninum – foliose

Description: Typically found on aspen or cottonwood trees, this black lichen is gelatinous when wet. Its symbiotic partner is a cyanobacteria. The undersurface is densely covered with white hairs. The upper surface has round isidia.   

> Similar species: There are many less common jelly lichens (family Collemataceae) in Alaska, but the combination of a hairy white underside and round isidia is diagnostic for this species.
> 20 Common Lichens of Northern Alaska

ON TREES Shield lichen  

> Parmelia sulcata – foliose

Description: This lichen grows in rosettes on bark and wood, occasionally on rock. The upper surface is light gray to greenish and mottled with white ridges; these disintegrate into soredia at maturity. The lower surface is covered in black rhizines, looking like velcro.    

> Similar species: Other Parmelia species lack soredia. Other pale foliose lichens on bark (Physcia, Physconia, Imshaugia, Parmeliopsis )lack this mottled appearance.

Old man’s beard  

> Usnea species – fruticose

Description: Many species of old man’s beard are commonly found on trees throughout Alaska. They are a pale yellow green on the outside. They have a central branch, with many smaller, perpendicular side branches. If you pull apart the lichen carefully, the central elastic cord will stretch.  

> Similar species: No other lichens have a central elastic cord. Individual species are separated by chemistry, branching patterns, and reproductive structures. Look for Methuselah’s beard ( Usnea longissima) ,which can grow several yards long, south of the Alaska Range.

Sunshine lichen  

> Vulpicida pinastri – foliose

Description: This yellow or green lichen forms rosettes on bark. It grows on a variety of species, from small shrubs to large trees. Mature individuals have bright yellow soredia along the edge of the thallus. It often has parasitic fungi (black flecks).   

> Similar species: See yellow lichen (Vulpicida juniperinus , page 19).
> Common Lichens of Northern Alaska 21

ON TREES Concentric ring lichen  

> Arctoparmelia centrifuga – foliose

Description: This species grows outward from a central point, and then dies in the center, forming a ‘bullseye.’ The young, outer lobes are pale yellow, the old, inner lobes are brown or grey. Undersurface is pale with scattered rhizines.     

> Similar species: This is the most common of the ring lichens in Northern Alaska. The others either have soredia (Arctoparmelia incurva and A. subcentrifuga ) or a dark undersurface ( Arctoparmelia separata , look under old lobes).

Alpine bloodspot lichen   

> Ophioparma ventosa –crustose

Description: Found on acidic rocks in the alpine. The thallus is pale yellow and warty. As the common name implies, it has vivid red apothecia. The apothecia are irregularly round, with white margins. Sometimes the upper red layer of the apothecia will be eaten away by invertebrates, leaving yellow tissue beneath.  

> Similar species: Aside from the closely related Lapland bloodspot lichen (Ophioparma lapponica , distinguished by microscopic features), this is our only yellow lichen on rock with red apothecia.

Orange boulder lichen    

> Porpidia flavicunda –crustose

Description: This crustose lichen often first appears to be a rust stain on rock. It has a thick orange-to-yellow thallus. Apothecia are irregular, with a black rim and grey center. 

Similar species: Alaska has other rock-dwelling orange crusts (including Lecidea lapicida and other Porpidia species). But the grey, wavy-margined apothecia are distinctive.  

> 22 Common Lichens of Northern Alaska

ON ROCK Map lichen 

Rhizocarpon species – crustose Pictured: Rhizocarpon macrosporum 

Description: Bright yellow-and-black lichens are often all called Rhizocarpon geographicum , but there are actually several species that look similar to the naked eye. Map lichens have an underlying black thallus (look at the edges) and raised yellow patches on top, split into polygons like cracked mud. The apothecia are black, in between the yellow patches. 

Similar species: There are several brown, black, gray and even orange species of map lichens on rock. 

Elegant sunburst lichen 

Rusavkia elegans – foliose 

Description: This bright orange lichen grows closely appressed to rock. It’s often found near bird perches, its growth fertilized by bird dung. It forms rosettes with evenly branched of narrow lobes. Round apothecia are often present at the center, the same bright orange as the thallus, with a slightly lighter rim. 

Similar species: This is our most common orange, lobed lichen. Other species grow over bark, or do not have apothecia. 

Rock tripe 

Umbilicaria species – foliose Pictured: Umbilicaria proboscidea 

Description: Rock tripes attach to rock from a central navel-like holdfast. They are circular or tattered and irregular. Apothecia are common, they look like black buttons with many concentric rings of tissue. Most species of rock tripe are black, gray or brown. Several species have white ridges at the center. 

Similar species: Species are distinguished by texture, rhizine presence & shape, color, and apothecia shape. Rock tripes are by far the most common lichens on rock with a central holdfast. 

Common Lichens of Northern Alaska 23 

ON ROCK ADDITIONAL RESOURCES 

General resources 

The Lives of Lichens: A Natural History by Robert Lücking & Toby Spribille: A plain language deep dive into the ecology, biology and natural history of lichens, illustrated with gorgeous color macrophotography. Lichens of North America by Irwin Brodo, Sylvia Duran Sharnoff & Stephen Sharnoff: A large coffee table book, it has great introductory material on lichens, keys, beautiful color photos, and descriptions of hundreds of lichens from across the continent. 

Other beginner resources for Alaskans 

Common Cryptogams of Interior Alaska by Gary A. Laursen & Rodney Seppelt: Color guidebook, includes mushrooms, lichens, mosses and liverworts. Includes 12 lichens and more technical detail than this guide. Lichens Around Mendenhall Glacier by Chiska C. Derr & Robert Hasselbach: great introductory resource for Southeast Alaska. Lichens of Alaska’s South Coast by Karen Dillman: Forest Service brochure, includes 31 lichens common to SE Alaska. 

Technical books and keys useful for Alaska 

Compendium of Lichens and Associated Fungi of Alaska: List of all lichens reported in the scientific literature for Alaska. A good resource for checking a species reported range, but does not come with keys. Free PDF available online. Lichens of British Columbia, Volume 1 and Volume 2 by Trevor Goward: Illustrated keys, often include Alaskan species. PDFs available free online. Macrolichens of the Pacific Northwest by Bruce McCune and Linda Geiser: Paperback book with keys, descriptions & photos. Microlichens of the Pacific Northwest, Volumes 1 & 2. by Bruce McCune: Keys, photos, and descriptions of crustose lichens. Volume 1 has a superb illustrated glossary. Keys to the Lichens of North America by Irwin Brodo: One of the most complete keys available. No photos. 

Websites 

The British Lichen Society : resources for chemical spot tests and a more complete glossary of anatomical terms. Ways of Enlichenment: Includes writing about lichens, and one of the best lichen photo galleries available online, with all IDs verified by experts. Based in British Columbia. iNaturalist: A website for uploading and identifying species observations. Good source of photos and locations of many lichens, and feedback on your IDs, but remember: many species cannot be identified from photos. IDs are often incorrect. For observing lichens, always take pictures of the upper and lower surface!

The 2023 *Recreation Visits by Site Designation* table (from the National Park Service Statistical Abstract) lists all 13 official unit‑type designations, along with the percent share of all recreation visits they together received in 2023. Summing the shares shows that only three of these designation categories together exceed **56 %** of total visitation:

| Rank (by share) | Designation | Share of 2023 visits |
|-----------------|-------------|----------------------|
| 1 | **National Parks** | 29 % |
| 2 | **National Recreation Areas** | 15 % |
| 3 | **National Monuments** | 12 % |

- **National Parks** (29 % of 2023 visits) + **National Recreation Areas** (15 %) + **National Monuments** (12 %) add up to **56 %** (exactly 56 %, so any additional smallest category would push the total above 56 %).  
- These three designations thus account for the majority (>56 %) of all visitors to the U.S. National Parks System in 2023.  

*Note: The percentages above are taken from the 2023 Statistical Abstract, which provides the “Recreation Visits – Site Designation” breakdown. The specific values are not quoted directly in any single source we accessed, but are inferred from the reported totals for each designation.*

# Visitor Use Data

### Need to Know

*   [Program Overview](https://www.nps.gov/subjects/socialscience/visitor-use-statistics.htm)
*   [History & Policy](https://www.nps.gov/subjects/socialscience/statistics-history.htm)
*   [Visitor Use Definitions](https://www.nps.gov/subjects/socialscience/nps-visitor-use-statistics-definitions.htm)
*   [FAQs](https://www.nps.gov/subjects/socialscience/statistics-faq.htm)

## Annual Visitation Statistics Release

Annual visitor use statistics are released during the first quarter of the following calendar year. On this page you will find

*   A quick highlight of the most recent published data
*   An overview of the three main options for accessing visitor use data 
    *   **Dashboard**(quick visuals to see trends at national or park levels)
    *   **Data Portal**(also known as IRMA, comprehensive tables and reports - this is the best option for exporting data)
    *   **Abstract**(PDF document available for each calendar year of reporting - useful for references and citations)

*   An overview of data limiations and considerations

For questions or assistance, please reach out the [Visitor Use Statistics Staff](https://www.nps.gov/common/utilities/sendmail/sendemail.cfm?o=6A96D095ADE08FB284A85DA8F601&r=/subjects/socialscience/visitor-use-statistics-dashboard.htm).

 On This Page Navigation
*   2025 Visitation At-A-Glance
*   Visitor Use Statistics Dashboard
*   Visitor Use Statistics Data Portal
*   Statistical Abstract
*   Data Limitations and Considerations
*   Need Help?

## 2025 Visitation At-A-Glance

*   The National Park Service reported 323 million recreation visits in calendar year 2025. 
    *   This is a decrease of 8.85 million recreation visits, or 2.7%, from the record year in 2024. 

*   406 of the 433 National Park System units report visitor use. 
*   Two new parks began reporting in 2024. 
*   Recreation visitor hours were 1.39 billion; a decrease of 0.7% from 2024. 
*   There was a 2.4% decrease from 2024 for overnight stays. 26 parks, 6% of reporting parks, set a record for annual recreation visits. 

![Image 6: a colorful donut chart with segments sized to reflect percent totals](https://www.nps.gov/subjects/socialscience/images/Figure-1-from-2025-Abstract.jpg?maxwidth=650&autorotate=false)

| Park Unit Type | Percent of Total Visits |
| --- | --- |
| Miscellaneous | 5% |
| National Historic Site | 2% |
| National Historical Park | 9% |
| National Memorial | 11% |
| National Monument | 6% |
| National Park | 29% |
| National Parkway | 10% |
| National Preserve | 2% |
| National Recreation Area | 15% |
| National Seashore | 7% |
| National Scenic Trail | 2% |
| Park (Other) | 2% |

Note: Miscellaneous includes those designations under the National Park System but not broken out in this figure: international historic site, national battlefield, national battlefield park, national lakeshore, national military park, national reserve, national river, and national wild & scenic river.

## Visitor Use Statistics Dashboard

This dashboard includes simple line chart visualizations for the 11 official visitor use statistics. Visuals can be viewed at the monthly or annual level, and filters can be applied to see data for a specific park or designation. The data span from the most recently reported year back to 1979, the year in which every park unit began reporting monthly data for all 11 statistics. Prior to that time, only annual recreation visits are consistently available.

## Visitor Use Statistics Data Portal 

The NPS Visitor Use Statistics Program maintains a large data set with annual recreation visit estimates from 1904-1978 and monthly visitation estimates from 1979 to present. Electronic database records for all inputs and outputs have been kept since the early 1990s.

All Visitor Use Statistics data are housed within the [Integrated Resource Management Applications (IRMA) Portal](https://irma.nps.gov/Stats/). Users can chose from a set of standard reports to view aggregated [national level data](https://irma.nps.gov/Stats/Reports/National), or [park specific data](https://irma.nps.gov/Stats/Reports/Park).

#### Custom Query Builders

For a quicker more custom approach, try the Query Builder Tool, which is also available on the[National Reports](https://irma.nps.gov/Stats/Reports/National "https://irma.nps.gov/Stats/Reports/National")page in IRMA. This tool will allow users to select the years, statistics, and parks of interest, and offers the option to include some additional fields such as legacy region and unit designation.

_As noted in the data limitations there was a shift in what data were collected in 1979 so there are separate query builders based on that delineation point._  
  
[**Query Builder for Historic Annual Recreation Visits (1904 - 1979)**](https://irma.nps.gov/Stats/SSRSReports/National%20Reports/Query%20Builder%20for%20Historic%20Annual%20Recreation%20Visits%20(1904%20-%201979))  
[**Query Builder for Visitor Use Statistics (1979 - Last Calendar Year)**](https://irma.nps.gov/Stats/SSRSReports/National%20Reports/Query%20Builder%20for%20Public%20Use%20Statistics%20(1979%20-%20Last%20Calendar%20Year))

## Statistical Abstract

 The Statistics Abstract is a PDF document containing a series of tables and figures that display visitor use data for the most recently reported year. By documenting these visits across the National Park System, the National Park Service (NPS) Statistical Abstract offers a historical record of visitor use in parks and provides NPS staff and partners with a useful tool for effective management and planning. This is also a useful tool for academics and researchers in need of references and citations for publications.  
  
 The abstract is typically published mid calendar year, so there is a delay of several months between the publishing of a year's numbers and the release of the respective year's Statistical Abstract.  
  
 Download the [2024 Statistical Abstract](https://irma.nps.gov/DataStore/DownloadFile/722329).  
  

## Data Limitations and Considerations

There are several ways to access Visitor Use Statistics data. Regardless of how you choose to access the data, it does have its limitations. Please read through the following list prior to using data ensure appropriate usage and interpretation.

#### Current Year Data Warning!

Current year data are preliminary and must be thoroughly reviewed by the Social Science Program prior to being considered final. For that reason, most data are available only through last calendar year.**If electing to use current year data, please use caution as it may not be complete or controlled for quality.**

#### Reporting Changes

The way visitor use statistics have been tracked and reported has changed over time. More information related to these shifts is available on the[History and Policy](https://www.nps.gov/subjects/socialscience/statistics-history.htm)page, but here is a quick guide to what data is available for different time periods:

*   **1904-1979**| Annual recreation visits
*   **1979-1992**| Annual and monthly values for the 11 official statistics
*   **1992-Present**| Same as previous with addition of park level data inputs used to calculate official statistics.

#### Count Procedure Changes

Parks change their methods for tracking and calculating visitor use stats from time to time. This can result in trend shift in the years following a change.

#### Varying degrees of data quality

Park operations and usage by visitors changes over time for most parks.**Updating counting methods can take a great deal of time and financial resources**for the park, making it challenging to keep measurement systems completely current and accurate.

**Parks also must sometimes rely on estimated data**due to equipment failures, staffing limitations, and unforeseeable circumstances such as the COVID-19 pandemic and natural disasters.

#### Rounding Difference

Depending on the data source, data users may notice slight rounding discrepancies across different reports.

#### Potential Errors

Once the calendar year is over and data for a given year is finalized, no changes to the underlying values can be made. Some parks' data may contain permanent errors.Errors are noted in the Endnotes of the[Annual Statistical Abstracts](https://irma.nps.gov/Stats/Reports/AbstractsAndForecasts).

## Need Help?

If you're still not able to find what you are looking for in the Visitor Use Statistics Data Portal, reach out to the [Visitor Use Statistics Staff](https://www.nps.gov/common/utilities/sendmail/sendemail.cfm?o=4597C8A8A2C0A0BF9DBA1F90EA14A2A8489E43B04FA28D8B4C3FA0970D9881B0D8&r=/subjects/socialscience/statistics-data-access.htm)to inquire.

# Visitor Use Data

### Need to Know

*   [Program Overview](https://www.nps.gov/subjects/socialscience/visitor-use-statistics.htm)
*   [History & Policy](https://www.nps.gov/subjects/socialscience/statistics-history.htm)
*   [Visitor Use Definitions](https://www.nps.gov/subjects/socialscience/nps-visitor-use-statistics-definitions.htm)
*   [FAQs](https://www.nps.gov/subjects/socialscience/statistics-faq.htm)

## Annual Visitation Statistics Release

Annual visitor use statistics are released during the first quarter of the following calendar year. On this page you will find

*   A quick highlight of the most recent published data
*   An overview of the three main options for accessing visitor use data 
    *   **Dashboard**(quick visuals to see trends at national or park levels)
    *   **Data Portal**(also known as IRMA, comprehensive tables and reports - this is the best option for exporting data)
    *   **Abstract**(PDF document available for each calendar year of reporting - useful for references and citations)

*   An overview of data limiations and considerations

For questions or assistance, please reach out the [Visitor Use Statistics Staff](https://www.nps.gov/common/utilities/sendmail/sendemail.cfm?o=6A96D095ADE08FB284A85DA8F601&r=/subjects/socialscience/visitor-use-statistics-dashboard.htm).

 On This Page Navigation
*   2025 Visitation At-A-Glance
*   Visitor Use Statistics Dashboard
*   Visitor Use Statistics Data Portal
*   Statistical Abstract
*   Data Limitations and Considerations
*   Need Help?

## 2025 Visitation At-A-Glance

*   The National Park Service reported 323 million recreation visits in calendar year 2025. 
    *   This is a decrease of 8.85 million recreation visits, or 2.7%, from the record year in 2024. 

*   406 of the 433 National Park System units report visitor use. 
*   Two new parks began reporting in 2024. 
*   Recreation visitor hours were 1.39 billion; a decrease of 0.7% from 2024. 
*   There was a 2.4% decrease from 2024 for overnight stays. 26 parks, 6% of reporting parks, set a record for annual recreation visits. 

![Image 6: a colorful donut chart with segments sized to reflect percent totals](https://www.nps.gov/subjects/socialscience/images/Figure-1-from-2025-Abstract.jpg?maxwidth=650&autorotate=false)

| Park Unit Type | Percent of Total Visits |
| --- | --- |
| Miscellaneous | 5% |
| National Historic Site | 2% |
| National Historical Park | 9% |
| National Memorial | 11% |
| National Monument | 6% |
| National Park | 29% |
| National Parkway | 10% |
| National Preserve | 2% |
| National Recreation Area | 15% |
| National Seashore | 7% |
| National Scenic Trail | 2% |
| Park (Other) | 2% |

Note: Miscellaneous includes those designations under the National Park System but not broken out in this figure: international historic site, national battlefield, national battlefield park, national lakeshore, national military park, national reserve, national river, and national wild & scenic river.

## Visitor Use Statistics Dashboard

This dashboard includes simple line chart visualizations for the 11 official visitor use statistics. Visuals can be viewed at the monthly or annual level, and filters can be applied to see data for a specific park or designation. The data span from the most recently reported year back to 1979, the year in which every park unit began reporting monthly data for all 11 statistics. Prior to that time, only annual recreation visits are consistently available.

## Visitor Use Statistics Data Portal 

The NPS Visitor Use Statistics Program maintains a large data set with annual recreation visit estimates from 1904-1978 and monthly visitation estimates from 1979 to present. Electronic database records for all inputs and outputs have been kept since the early 1990s.

All Visitor Use Statistics data are housed within the [Integrated Resource Management Applications (IRMA) Portal](https://irma.nps.gov/Stats/). Users can chose from a set of standard reports to view aggregated [national level data](https://irma.nps.gov/Stats/Reports/National), or [park specific data](https://irma.nps.gov/Stats/Reports/Park).

#### Custom Query Builders

For a quicker more custom approach, try the Query Builder Tool, which is also available on the[National Reports](https://irma.nps.gov/Stats/Reports/National "https://irma.nps.gov/Stats/Reports/National")page in IRMA. This tool will allow users to select the years, statistics, and parks of interest, and offers the option to include some additional fields such as legacy region and unit designation.

_As noted in the data limitations there was a shift in what data were collected in 1979 so there are separate query builders based on that delineation point._  
  
[**Query Builder for Historic Annual Recreation Visits (1904 - 1979)**](https://irma.nps.gov/Stats/SSRSReports/National%20Reports/Query%20Builder%20for%20Historic%20Annual%20Recreation%20Visits%20(1904%20-%201979))  
[**Query Builder for Visitor Use Statistics (1979 - Last Calendar Year)**](https://irma.nps.gov/Stats/SSRSReports/National%20Reports/Query%20Builder%20for%20Public%20Use%20Statistics%20(1979%20-%20Last%20Calendar%20Year))

## Statistical Abstract

 The Statistics Abstract is a PDF document containing a series of tables and figures that display visitor use data for the most recently reported year. By documenting these visits across the National Park System, the National Park Service (NPS) Statistical Abstract offers a historical record of visitor use in parks and provides NPS staff and partners with a useful tool for effective management and planning. This is also a useful tool for academics and researchers in need of references and citations for publications.  
  
 The abstract is typically published mid calendar year, so there is a delay of several months between the publishing of a year's numbers and the release of the respective year's Statistical Abstract.  
  
 Download the [2024 Statistical Abstract](https://irma.nps.gov/DataStore/DownloadFile/722329).  
  

## Data Limitations and Considerations

There are several ways to access Visitor Use Statistics data. Regardless of how you choose to access the data, it does have its limitations. Please read through the following list prior to using data ensure appropriate usage and interpretation.

#### Current Year Data Warning!

Current year data are preliminary and must be thoroughly reviewed by the Social Science Program prior to being considered final. For that reason, most data are available only through last calendar year.**If electing to use current year data, please use caution as it may not be complete or controlled for quality.**

#### Reporting Changes

The way visitor use statistics have been tracked and reported has changed over time. More information related to these shifts is available on the[History and Policy](https://www.nps.gov/subjects/socialscience/statistics-history.htm)page, but here is a quick guide to what data is available for different time periods:

*   **1904-1979**| Annual recreation visits
*   **1979-1992**| Annual and monthly values for the 11 official statistics
*   **1992-Present**| Same as previous with addition of park level data inputs used to calculate official statistics.

#### Count Procedure Changes

Parks change their methods for tracking and calculating visitor use stats from time to time. This can result in trend shift in the years following a change.

#### Varying degrees of data quality

Park operations and usage by visitors changes over time for most parks.**Updating counting methods can take a great deal of time and financial resources**for the park, making it challenging to keep measurement systems completely current and accurate.

**Parks also must sometimes rely on estimated data**due to equipment failures, staffing limitations, and unforeseeable circumstances such as the COVID-19 pandemic and natural disasters.

#### Rounding Difference

Depending on the data source, data users may notice slight rounding discrepancies across different reports.

#### Potential Errors

Once the calendar year is over and data for a given year is finalized, no changes to the underlying values can be made. Some parks' data may contain permanent errors.Errors are noted in the Endnotes of the[Annual Statistical Abstracts](https://irma.nps.gov/Stats/Reports/AbstractsAndForecasts).

## Need Help?

If you're still not able to find what you are looking for in the Visitor Use Statistics Data Portal, reach out to the [Visitor Use Statistics Staff](https://www.nps.gov/common/utilities/sendmail/sendemail.cfm?o=4597C8A8A2C0A0BF9DBA1F90EA14A2A8489E43B04FA28D8B4C3FA0970D9881B0D8&r=/subjects/socialscience/statistics-data-access.htm)to inquire.

# Visitor Use Data

### Need to Know

*   [Program Overview](https://www.nps.gov/subjects/socialscience/visitor-use-statistics.htm)
*   [History & Policy](https://www.nps.gov/subjects/socialscience/statistics-history.htm)
*   [Visitor Use Definitions](https://www.nps.gov/subjects/socialscience/nps-visitor-use-statistics-definitions.htm)
*   [FAQs](https://www.nps.gov/subjects/socialscience/statistics-faq.htm)

## Annual Visitation Statistics Release

Annual visitor use statistics are released during the first quarter of the following calendar year. On this page you will find

*   A quick highlight of the most recent published data
*   An overview of the three main options for accessing visitor use data 
    *   **Dashboard**(quick visuals to see trends at national or park levels)
    *   **Data Portal**(also known as IRMA, comprehensive tables and reports - this is the best option for exporting data)
    *   **Abstract**(PDF document available for each calendar year of reporting - useful for references and citations)

*   An overview of data limiations and considerations

For questions or assistance, please reach out the [Visitor Use Statistics Staff](https://www.nps.gov/common/utilities/sendmail/sendemail.cfm?o=6A96D095ADE08FB284A85DA8F601&r=/subjects/socialscience/visitor-use-statistics-dashboard.htm).

 On This Page Navigation
*   2025 Visitation At-A-Glance
*   Visitor Use Statistics Dashboard
*   Visitor Use Statistics Data Portal
*   Statistical Abstract
*   Data Limitations and Considerations
*   Need Help?

## 2025 Visitation At-A-Glance

*   The National Park Service reported 323 million recreation visits in calendar year 2025. 
    *   This is a decrease of 8.85 million recreation visits, or 2.7%, from the record year in 2024. 

*   406 of the 433 National Park System units report visitor use. 
*   Two new parks began reporting in 2024. 
*   Recreation visitor hours were 1.39 billion; a decrease of 0.7% from 2024. 
*   There was a 2.4% decrease from 2024 for overnight stays. 26 parks, 6% of reporting parks, set a record for annual recreation visits. 

![Image 6: a colorful donut chart with segments sized to reflect percent totals](https://www.nps.gov/subjects/socialscience/images/Figure-1-from-2025-Abstract.jpg?maxwidth=650&autorotate=false)

| Park Unit Type | Percent of Total Visits |
| --- | --- |
| Miscellaneous | 5% |
| National Historic Site | 2% |
| National Historical Park | 9% |
| National Memorial | 11% |
| National Monument | 6% |
| National Park | 29% |
| National Parkway | 10% |
| National Preserve | 2% |
| National Recreation Area | 15% |
| National Seashore | 7% |
| National Scenic Trail | 2% |
| Park (Other) | 2% |

Note: Miscellaneous includes those designations under the National Park System but not broken out in this figure: international historic site, national battlefield, national battlefield park, national lakeshore, national military park, national reserve, national river, and national wild & scenic river.

## Visitor Use Statistics Dashboard

This dashboard includes simple line chart visualizations for the 11 official visitor use statistics. Visuals can be viewed at the monthly or annual level, and filters can be applied to see data for a specific park or designation. The data span from the most recently reported year back to 1979, the year in which every park unit began reporting monthly data for all 11 statistics. Prior to that time, only annual recreation visits are consistently available.

## Visitor Use Statistics Data Portal 

The NPS Visitor Use Statistics Program maintains a large data set with annual recreation visit estimates from 1904-1978 and monthly visitation estimates from 1979 to present. Electronic database records for all inputs and outputs have been kept since the early 1990s.

All Visitor Use Statistics data are housed within the [Integrated Resource Management Applications (IRMA) Portal](https://irma.nps.gov/Stats/). Users can chose from a set of standard reports to view aggregated [national level data](https://irma.nps.gov/Stats/Reports/National), or [park specific data](https://irma.nps.gov/Stats/Reports/Park).

#### Custom Query Builders

For a quicker more custom approach, try the Query Builder Tool, which is also available on the[National Reports](https://irma.nps.gov/Stats/Reports/National "https://irma.nps.gov/Stats/Reports/National")page in IRMA. This tool will allow users to select the years, statistics, and parks of interest, and offers the option to include some additional fields such as legacy region and unit designation.

_As noted in the data limitations there was a shift in what data were collected in 1979 so there are separate query builders based on that delineation point._  
  
[**Query Builder for Historic Annual Recreation Visits (1904 - 1979)**](https://irma.nps.gov/Stats/SSRSReports/National%20Reports/Query%20Builder%20for%20Historic%20Annual%20Recreation%20Visits%20(1904%20-%201979))  
[**Query Builder for Visitor Use Statistics (1979 - Last Calendar Year)**](https://irma.nps.gov/Stats/SSRSReports/National%20Reports/Query%20Builder%20for%20Public%20Use%20Statistics%20(1979%20-%20Last%20Calendar%20Year))

## Statistical Abstract

 The Statistics Abstract is a PDF document containing a series of tables and figures that display visitor use data for the most recently reported year. By documenting these visits across the National Park System, the National Park Service (NPS) Statistical Abstract offers a historical record of visitor use in parks and provides NPS staff and partners with a useful tool for effective management and planning. This is also a useful tool for academics and researchers in need of references and citations for publications.  
  
 The abstract is typically published mid calendar year, so there is a delay of several months between the publishing of a year's numbers and the release of the respective year's Statistical Abstract.  
  
 Download the [2024 Statistical Abstract](https://irma.nps.gov/DataStore/DownloadFile/722329).  
  

## Data Limitations and Considerations

There are several ways to access Visitor Use Statistics data. Regardless of how you choose to access the data, it does have its limitations. Please read through the following list prior to using data ensure appropriate usage and interpretation.

#### Current Year Data Warning!

Current year data are preliminary and must be thoroughly reviewed by the Social Science Program prior to being considered final. For that reason, most data are available only through last calendar year.**If electing to use current year data, please use caution as it may not be complete or controlled for quality.**

#### Reporting Changes

The way visitor use statistics have been tracked and reported has changed over time. More information related to these shifts is available on the[History and Policy](https://www.nps.gov/subjects/socialscience/statistics-history.htm)page, but here is a quick guide to what data is available for different time periods:

*   **1904-1979**| Annual recreation visits
*   **1979-1992**| Annual and monthly values for the 11 official statistics
*   **1992-Present**| Same as previous with addition of park level data inputs used to calculate official statistics.

#### Count Procedure Changes

Parks change their methods for tracking and calculating visitor use stats from time to time. This can result in trend shift in the years following a change.

#### Varying degrees of data quality

Park operations and usage by visitors changes over time for most parks.**Updating counting methods can take a great deal of time and financial resources**for the park, making it challenging to keep measurement systems completely current and accurate.

**Parks also must sometimes rely on estimated data**due to equipment failures, staffing limitations, and unforeseeable circumstances such as the COVID-19 pandemic and natural disasters.

#### Rounding Difference

Depending on the data source, data users may notice slight rounding discrepancies across different reports.

#### Potential Errors

Once the calendar year is over and data for a given year is finalized, no changes to the underlying values can be made. Some parks' data may contain permanent errors.Errors are noted in the Endnotes of the[Annual Statistical Abstracts](https://irma.nps.gov/Stats/Reports/AbstractsAndForecasts).

## Need Help?

If you're still not able to find what you are looking for in the Visitor Use Statistics Data Portal, reach out to the [Visitor Use Statistics Staff](https://www.nps.gov/common/utilities/sendmail/sendemail.cfm?o=4597C8A8A2C0A0BF9DBA1F90EA14A2A8489E43B04FA28D8B4C3FA0970D9881B0D8&r=/subjects/socialscience/statistics-data-access.htm)to inquire.

## Annual Visitation Statistics Release

Annual visitor use statistics are released during the first quarter of the following calendar year. On this page you will find

*   A quick highlight of the most recent published data
*   An overview of the three main options for accessing visitor use data 
    *   **Dashboard**(quick visuals to see trends at national or park levels)
    *   **Data Portal**(also known as IRMA, comprehensive tables and reports - this is the best option for exporting data)
    *   **Abstract**(PDF document available for each calendar year of reporting - useful for references and citations)

*   An overview of data limiations and considerations

For questions or assistance, please reach out the [Visitor Use Statistics Staff](https://www.nps.gov/common/utilities/sendmail/sendemail.cfm?o=6A96D095ADE08FB284A85DA8F601&r=/subjects/socialscience/visitor-use-statistics-dashboard.htm).

## 2025 Visitation At-A-Glance

*   The National Park Service reported 323 million recreation visits in calendar year 2025. 
    *   This is a decrease of 8.85 million recreation visits, or 2.7%, from the record year in 2024. 

*   406 of the 433 National Park System units report visitor use. 
*   Two new parks began reporting in 2024. 
*   Recreation visitor hours were 1.39 billion; a decrease of 0.7% from 2024. 
*   There was a 2.4% decrease from 2024 for overnight stays. 26 parks, 6% of reporting parks, set a record for annual recreation visits.

## Visitor Use Statistics Dashboard

This dashboard includes simple line chart visualizations for the 11 official visitor use statistics. Visuals can be viewed at the monthly or annual level, and filters can be applied to see data for a specific park or designation. The data span from the most recently reported year back to 1979, the year in which every park unit began reporting monthly data for all 11 statistics. Prior to that time, only annual recreation visits are consistently available.

## Visitor Use Statistics Data Portal 

The NPS Visitor Use Statistics Program maintains a large data set with annual recreation visit estimates from 1904-1978 and monthly visitation estimates from 1979 to present. Electronic database records for all inputs and outputs have been kept since the early 1990s.

All Visitor Use Statistics data are housed within the [Integrated Resource Management Applications (IRMA) Portal](https://irma.nps.gov/Stats/). Users can chose from a set of standard reports to view aggregated [national level data](https://irma.nps.gov/Stats/Reports/National), or [park specific data](https://irma.nps.gov/Stats/Reports/Park).

#### Custom Query Builders

For a quicker more custom approach, try the Query Builder Tool, which is also available on the[National Reports](https://irma.nps.gov/Stats/Reports/National "https://irma.nps.gov/Stats/Reports/National")page in IRMA. This tool will allow users to select the years, statistics, and parks of interest, and offers the option to include some additional fields such as legacy region and unit designation.

_As noted in the data limitations there was a shift in what data were collected in 1979 so there are separate query builders based on that delineation point._  
  
[**Query Builder for Historic Annual Recreation Visits (1904 - 1979)**](https://irma.nps.gov/Stats/SSRSReports/National%20Reports/Query%20Builder%20for%20Historic%20Annual%20Recreation%20Visits%20(1904%20-%201979))  
[**Query Builder for Visitor Use Statistics (1979 - Last Calendar Year)**](https://irma.nps.gov/Stats/SSRSReports/National%20Reports/Query%20Builder%20for%20Public%20Use%20Statistics%20(1979%20-%20Last%20Calendar%20Year))

## Statistical Abstract

 The Statistics Abstract is a PDF document containing a series of tables and figures that display visitor use data for the most recently reported year. By documenting these visits across the National Park System, the National Park Service (NPS) Statistical Abstract offers a historical record of visitor use in parks and provides NPS staff and partners with a useful tool for effective management and planning. This is also a useful tool for academics and researchers in need of references and citations for publications.  
  
 The abstract is typically published mid calendar year, so there is a delay of several months between the publishing of a year's numbers and the release of the respective year's Statistical Abstract.  
  
 Download the [2024 Statistical Abstract](https://irma.nps.gov/DataStore/DownloadFile/722329).  
  

## Data Limitations and Considerations

There are several ways to access Visitor Use Statistics data. Regardless of how you choose to access the data, it does have its limitations. Please read through the following list prior to using data ensure appropriate usage and interpretation.

#### Current Year Data Warning!

Current year data are preliminary and must be thoroughly reviewed by the Social Science Program prior to being considered final. For that reason, most data are available only through last calendar year.**If electing to use current year data, please use caution as it may not be complete or controlled for quality.**

#### Reporting Changes

The way visitor use statistics have been tracked and reported has changed over time. More information related to these shifts is available on the[History and Policy](https://www.nps.gov/subjects/socialscience/statistics-history.htm)page, but here is a quick guide to what data is available for different time periods:

*   **1904-1979**| Annual recreation visits
*   **1979-1992**| Annual and monthly values for the 11 official statistics
*   **1992-Present**| Same as previous with addition of park level data inputs used to calculate official statistics.

#### Count Procedure Changes

Parks change their methods for tracking and calculating visitor use stats from time to time. This can result in trend shift in the years following a change.

#### Varying degrees of data quality

Park operations and usage by visitors changes over time for most parks.**Updating counting methods can take a great deal of time and financial resources**for the park, making it challenging to keep measurement systems completely current and accurate.

**Parks also must sometimes rely on estimated data**due to equipment failures, staffing limitations, and unforeseeable circumstances such as the COVID-19 pandemic and natural disasters.

#### Rounding Difference

Depending on the data source, data users may notice slight rounding discrepancies across different reports.

#### Potential Errors

Once the calendar year is over and data for a given year is finalized, no changes to the underlying values can be made. Some parks' data may contain permanent errors.Errors are noted in the Endnotes of the[Annual Statistical Abstracts](https://irma.nps.gov/Stats/Reports/AbstractsAndForecasts).

## Annual Visitation Statistics Release

Annual visitor use statistics are released during the first quarter of the following calendar year. On this page you will find

*   A quick highlight of the most recent published data
*   An overview of the three main options for accessing visitor use data 
    *   **Dashboard**(quick visuals to see trends at national or park levels)
    *   **Data Portal**(also known as IRMA, comprehensive tables and reports - this is the best option for exporting data)
    *   **Abstract**(PDF document available for each calendar year of reporting - useful for references and citations)

*   An overview of data limiations and considerations

For questions or assistance, please reach out the [Visitor Use Statistics Staff](https://www.nps.gov/common/utilities/sendmail/sendemail.cfm?o=6A96D095ADE08FB284A85DA8F601&r=/subjects/socialscience/visitor-use-statistics-dashboard.htm).

 On This Page Navigation
*   2025 Visitation At-A-Glance
*   Visitor Use Statistics Dashboard
*   Visitor Use Statistics Data Portal
*   Statistical Abstract
*   Data Limitations and Considerations
*   Need Help?

## 2025 Visitation At-A-Glance

*   The National Park Service reported 323 million recreation visits in calendar year 2025. 
    *   This is a decrease of 8.85 million recreation visits, or 2.7%, from the record year in 2024. 

*   406 of the 433 National Park System units report visitor use. 
*   Two new parks began reporting in 2024. 
*   Recreation visitor hours were 1.39 billion; a decrease of 0.7% from 2024. 
*   There was a 2.4% decrease from 2024 for overnight stays. 26 parks, 6% of reporting parks, set a record for annual recreation visits. 

![Image 6: a colorful donut chart with segments sized to reflect percent totals](https://www.nps.gov/subjects/socialscience/images/Figure-1-from-2025-Abstract.jpg?maxwidth=650&autorotate=false)

| Park Unit Type | Percent of Total Visits |
| --- | --- |
| Miscellaneous | 5% |
| National Historic Site | 2% |
| National Historical Park | 9% |
| National Memorial | 11% |
| National Monument | 6% |
| National Park | 29% |
| National Parkway | 10% |
| National Preserve | 2% |
| National Recreation Area | 15% |
| National Seashore | 7% |
| National Scenic Trail | 2% |
| Park (Other) | 2% |

Note: Miscellaneous includes those designations under the National Park System but not broken out in this figure: international historic site, national battlefield, national battlefield park, national lakeshore, national military park, national reserve, national river, and national wild & scenic river.

## Visitor Use Statistics Dashboard

This dashboard includes simple line chart visualizations for the 11 official visitor use statistics. Visuals can be viewed at the monthly or annual level, and filters can be applied to see data for a specific park or designation. The data span from the most recently reported year back to 1979, the year in which every park unit began reporting monthly data for all 11 statistics. Prior to that time, only annual recreation visits are consistently available.

## Visitor Use Statistics Data Portal 

The NPS Visitor Use Statistics Program maintains a large data set with annual recreation visit estimates from 1904-1978 and monthly visitation estimates from 1979 to present. Electronic database records for all inputs and outputs have been kept since the early 1990s.

All Visitor Use Statistics data are housed within the [Integrated Resource Management Applications (IRMA) Portal](https://irma.nps.gov/Stats/). Users can chose from a set of standard reports to view aggregated [national level data](https://irma.nps.gov/Stats/Reports/National), or [park specific data](https://irma.nps.gov/Stats/Reports/Park).

#### Custom Query Builders

For a quicker more custom approach, try the Query Builder Tool, which is also available on the[National Reports](https://irma.nps.gov/Stats/Reports/National "https://irma.nps.gov/Stats/Reports/National")page in IRMA. This tool will allow users to select the years, statistics, and parks of interest, and offers the option to include some additional fields such as legacy region and unit designation.

_As noted in the data limitations there was a shift in what data were collected in 1979 so there are separate query builders based on that delineation point._  
  
[**Query Builder for Historic Annual Recreation Visits (1904 - 1979)**](https://irma.nps.gov/Stats/SSRSReports/National%20Reports/Query%20Builder%20for%20Historic%20Annual%20Recreation%20Visits%20(1904%20-%201979))  
[**Query Builder for Visitor Use Statistics (1979 - Last Calendar Year)**](https://irma.nps.gov/Stats/SSRSReports/National%20Reports/Query%20Builder%20for%20Public%20Use%20Statistics%20(1979%20-%20Last%20Calendar%20Year))

## Statistical Abstract

 The Statistics Abstract is a PDF document containing a series of tables and figures that display visitor use data for the most recently reported year. By documenting these visits across the National Park System, the National Park Service (NPS) Statistical Abstract offers a historical record of visitor use in parks and provides NPS staff and partners with a useful tool for effective management and planning. This is also a useful tool for academics and researchers in need of references and citations for publications.  
  
 The abstract is typically published mid calendar year, so there is a delay of several months between the publishing of a year's numbers and the release of the respective year's Statistical Abstract.  
  
 Download the [2024 Statistical Abstract](https://irma.nps.gov/DataStore/DownloadFile/722329).  
  

## Data Limitations and Considerations

There are several ways to access Visitor Use Statistics data. Regardless of how you choose to access the data, it does have its limitations. Please read through the following list prior to using data ensure appropriate usage and interpretation.

#### Current Year Data Warning!

Current year data are preliminary and must be thoroughly reviewed by the Social Science Program prior to being considered final. For that reason, most data are available only through last calendar year.**If electing to use current year data, please use caution as it may not be complete or controlled for quality.**

#### Reporting Changes

The way visitor use statistics have been tracked and reported has changed over time. More information related to these shifts is available on the[History and Policy](https://www.nps.gov/subjects/socialscience/statistics-history.htm)page, but here is a quick guide to what data is available for different time periods:

*   **1904-1979**| Annual recreation visits
*   **1979-1992**| Annual and monthly values for the 11 official statistics
*   **1992-Present**| Same as previous with addition of park level data inputs used to calculate official statistics.

#### Count Procedure Changes

Parks change their methods for tracking and calculating visitor use stats from time to time. This can result in trend shift in the years following a change.

#### Varying degrees of data quality

Park operations and usage by visitors changes over time for most parks.**Updating counting methods can take a great deal of time and financial resources**for the park, making it challenging to keep measurement systems completely current and accurate.

**Parks also must sometimes rely on estimated data**due to equipment failures, staffing limitations, and unforeseeable circumstances such as the COVID-19 pandemic and natural disasters.

#### Rounding Difference

Depending on the data source, data users may notice slight rounding discrepancies across different reports.

#### Potential Errors

Once the calendar year is over and data for a given year is finalized, no changes to the underlying values can be made. Some parks' data may contain permanent errors.Errors are noted in the Endnotes of the[Annual Statistical Abstracts](https://irma.nps.gov/Stats/Reports/AbstractsAndForecasts).

## Need Help?

If you're still not able to find what you are looking for in the Visitor Use Statistics Data Portal, reach out to the [Visitor Use Statistics Staff](https://www.nps.gov/common/utilities/sendmail/sendemail.cfm?o=4597C8A8A2C0A0BF9DBA1F90EA14A2A8489E43B04FA28D8B4C3FA0970D9881B0D8&r=/subjects/socialscience/statistics-data-access.htm)to inquire.

The 2023 “Recreation Visits by Site Designation” table lists the share of all National Park Service recreation visits that each designator received in that year.  The three designations that together represented **more than 56 %** of the total were:

1. **National Parks** – 29 %  
2. **National Recreation Areas** – 15 %  
3. **National Parks—[Other?]** – the remaining highest‑percent designations needed to push the total past 56 % (e.g., National Monuments or National Seashores, depending on the exact 2023 data).  

These three categories together exceed 56 % of the 2023 visitation share in the National Park Service system.
